title: MARTA: A ‘little’ black hole hidden in a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at 𝑧=3.8

paper.title: MARTA: A ‘little’ black hole hidden in a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at z = 3.8 z=3.8
paper.abstract:
ABSTRACT JWST has extended the search for accreting black holes into the high-redshift, low-mass regime, delivering unprecedented constraints on their formation path and seeding mechanisms.
Here we report the discovery of a low-mass black hole candidate in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 .
Combining deep JWST/NIRSpec MSA spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and archival VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy, we characterize the black hole, stellar host, and ionized gas properties of this system over the rest-frame UV-to-optical range.
We identify a broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component with L H ​ α , b = 2.35 × 10 41 L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=2.35\times 10^{41} erg s -1 and FWHM = 1270 − 250 + 260 {\rm FWHM}=1270^{+260}_{-250} km s -1 , with no [O iii ] counterpart of comparable width.
Under a broad-line-region interpretation, virial calibrations give log ⁡ ( M BH / M ⊙ ) = 6.52 − 0.23 + 0.18 \log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23} and λ Edd = L bol / L Edd = 0.07 \lambda_{\rm Edd}=L_{\rm bol}/L_{\rm Edd}=0.07 , or up to 0.38 0.38 for alternative calibrations.
The host is resolved into three compact clumps, with integrated SED fitting yielding log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) = 8.16 − 0.10 + 0.09 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10} .
The narrow-line spectrum is consistent with highly ionized, metal-poor gas, with 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) = 7.68 ± 0.04 12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm 0.04 ( ≃ 0.10 ​ Z ⊙ \simeq 0.10\,Z_{\odot} ).
The inferred M BH / M ⋆ = 2.3 % M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}=2.3\% lies approximately 2 dex above the extrapolated local relation between black-hole mass and host stellar mass, suggesting that black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed stellar component.
If black-hole growth began only when the first 10% of the observed stellar mass had formed ( t 10 = 92 t_{10}=92 Myr in lookback time) a 10 2 ​ M ⊙ 10^{2}\,M_{\odot} seed would require a lifetime-mean Eddington ratio ⟨ λ ⟩ ≃ 5.7 \langle\lambda\rangle\simeq 5.7 ; earlier growth or a more massive, e.g. direct-collapse black hole, seed would allow more moderate, sub-Eddington mean accretion.
In addition, MUSE data reveal extended Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission ( ≃ 6.5 \simeq 6.5 –6.9 proper kpc), offset by + 64 − 8 + 10 +64^{+10}_{-8} km s -1 from systemic, with a provisional escape fraction of ≃ 0.44 \simeq 0.44 .
Together with the narrow Mg II doublet ratio close to the optically thin limit and a high [O iii ]/[O ii ] ratio, these properties make MARTA 3887 a system in which black-hole growth, stellar assembly, and ionizing-photon escape can be studied jointly.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The origin of the first massive black holes remains a central problem in galaxy evolution. The existence of ∼ 10 9 ​ M ⊙ {\sim}10^{9}\,M_{\odot} quasars within the first billion years requires massive seeds, sustained near-Eddington accretion, super-Eddington episodes, or a combination of these processes ( Inayoshi et al., 2020 ) . Luminous quasars, however, sample only the high-mass tail of the distribution, while black holes with M BH ∼ 10 5 M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{5} – 10 7 ​ M ⊙ 10^{7}\,M_{\odot} in lower-mass galaxies provide complementary constraints on the early phases of seeding and black-hole-galaxy co-evolution. JWST/NIRSpec has extended the search and characterization of early black holes exactly into this regime. Broad-line AGN with M BH ∼ 10 6 M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{6} – 10 8 ​ M ⊙ 10^{8}\,M_{\odot} are now being routinely identified at high redshift, well below the luminosities accessible to pre-JWST quasar surveys ( Harikane et al., 2023 ; Kocevski et al., 2023 ; Larson et al., 2023 ; Übler et al., 2023 ; Matthee et al., 2024 ; Maiolino et al., 2024a ; Greene et al., 2024 ; Juodžbalis et al., 2026 ; Geris et al., 2026 ) . Many of the newly discovered black holes have large inferred M BH / M ⋆ M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star} ratios relative to local scaling relations ( Reines & Volonteri, 2015 ; Kormendy & Ho, 2013 ; Pacucci et al., 2023 ) , suggesting that black-hole growth might precede the assembly of the dominant stellar component. Strong selection effects related to flux and line-width sensitivity thresholds favour the detection of massive and/or rapidly accreting black holes at fixed host mass, while measurement scatter further enhances the detected upper envelope ( Lauer et al., 2007 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Selection-aware analyses indicate that the intrinsic high-redshift M BH M_{\rm BH} – M ⋆ M_{\star} relation may be consistent with the local relation, but with substantially larger scatter capable of producing the observed high- M BH / M ⋆ M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star} tail ( Ziparo et al., 2026 ) . Even if individual detections preferentially sample this upper envelope, the existence and frequency of such overmassive systems remain informative about black-hole formation and early growth. Models predict different low-mass distributions and scatter depending on their prescriptions for seeding, accretion, and feedback ( Habouzit et al., 2022 ; Volonteri et al., 2023 ; Trinca et al., 2026 ) ; well-characterized systems at the boundaries of the observed parameter space therefore provide complementary constraints on these processes. The identification of the faintest candidates requires particular care. Broad Balmer emission without an associated forbidden-line component of comparable width is a standard signature of a broad-line region (BLR), but at low luminosity it can also arise from interacting supernovae, shocks, outflows, or spatially unresolved galaxy structure ( Maiolino et al., 2025 ; Geris et al., 2026 ) . Classical optical narrow-line diagnostics are also poorly discriminating in the metal-poor, highly ionized ISM regime common at high redshift: metal-poor narrow-line regions overlap with the star-forming sequence, while extreme stellar populations can approach classical AGN-classification boundaries ( Feltre et al., 2016 ; Gutkin et al., 2016 ; Kewley et al., 2013 ; Mazzolari et al., 2024 ) . The combined effect of accretion supplying additional hard ionizing photons and radiative or mechanical AGN feedback lowering the neutral-gas covering fraction could open channels through which both AGN- and stellar-produced Lyman-continuum (LyC) photons can escape. However, this is not an inevitable consequence of hosting an AGN: simulations of high-redshift dwarf galaxies find that supernova feedback can dominate the structure of the ISM and that black-hole activity does not necessarily increase the LyC escape fraction ( Trebitsch et al., 2018 ) . Direct measurements at z ≃ 3 z\simeq 3 –4 span a broad range, from sub-unity average escape fractions in moderate-luminosity AGN to high values in luminous quasars ( Grazian et al., 2018 ; Iwata et al., 2022 ) . Compactness, high [O iii ]/[O ii ], and the presence of strong emission in resonant lines such as Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha and Mg II probing the physical conditions associated with low neutral gas column densities or porous sightlines can therefore test whether active black-hole growth coexists with favourable ionizing radiation escape channels ( Jaskot & Oey, 2013 ; Nakajima & Ouchi, 2014 ; Verhamme et al., 2015 ; Henry et al., 2018 ; Chisholm et al., 2020 ; Izotov et al., 2018 ; Flury et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Naidu et al., 2022 ) . Systems combining these features offer a view of the interplay between black-hole growth, stellar feedback, and ionizing radiation escape. Each proxy remains degenerate with stellar age, dust, gas geometry, and viewing angle, producing substantial scatter with f esc LyC f_{\rm esc}^{\rm LyC} ( Katz et al., 2022 ; Choustikov et al., 2024 ) . In this paper we present a multi-wavelength analysis of MARTA 3887, a compact, clumpy, and metal-poor galaxy at z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 with robust evidence for a low-mass black hole candidate, combining deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy. We investigate the origin of the detected H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha broad component, place the inferred black hole and host properties on scaling relations, and examine the implications for black-hole-galaxy co-evolution and for LyC escape. The paper is organized as follows. Sections 2 – 5 describe the data and measurements, Sect. 6 discusses the AGN interpretation, black-hole growth, and ionizing escape, and the final section summarizes our conclusions. We adopt the Planck 2018 cosmology throughout ( Planck Collaboration et al., 2020 ) . At z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 , 1 ′′ 1^{\prime\prime} corresponds to 7.28 proper kpc. sections.heading: 2.1 MARTA NIRSpec spectroscopy
sections.text: MARTA (Measuring Abundances at high Redshift with the T e T_{\rm e} Approach) is a JWST Cycle 1 GO programme (PID 1879, PI Curti) designed to obtain high-S/N rest-frame optical spectra of galaxies at cosmic noon and directly constrain their chemical abundances through faint auroral lines ( Cataldi et al., 2025 ) . A single JWST/NIRSpec micro-shutter-array (MSA) pointing in the COSMOS field targeted 127 galaxies ( Gardner et al., 2023 ; Rigby et al., 2023 ; Jakobsen et al., 2022 ; Ferruit et al., 2022 ) . The observing strategy combined a very deep G140M/F100LP exposure (31.6 h), optimized for [O iii ] λ ​ 4363 \lambda 4363 , with G235M/F170LP (7.3 h) coverage of the redder rest-optical spectrum and a shorter G235H/F170LP exposure (2.9 h) for resolved line kinematics. All configurations used three-shutter slitlets and a three-position nod along the slitlet. We reduced the data with the pipeline developed by the NIRSpec Instrument Team, adopted by the JADES collaboration, and described by Scholtz et al. (2026) 1 1 1 Fully reduced data for this programme can be found at https://jades.herts.ac.uk/other_GO/ . . Starting from the calibrated count-rate exposures, the workflow identifies contaminated or non-operational shutters, subtracts the background at pixel level using uncontaminated nod positions, extracts each target trace, applies the wavelength and spectrophotometric calibrations, rectifies and combines the exposures, and produces calibrated two- and one-dimensional spectra. The one-dimensional products use the standard point-source path-loss and slit-loss corrections; we retain the two-dimensional spectra to assess the resolved trace independently in Sect. 3 and Appendix B . A relevant feature of this reduction is the extraction and calibration of spectral traces beyond the nominal wavelength limits of each disperser/filter pair, wherever the detector still records non-negligible throughput. For G235M/F170LP the calibrated range is extended from the nominal red limit near 3.1 ​ μ 3.1\,\mu m to approximately 4.0 ​ μ 4.0\,\mu m ( Scholtz et al., 2026 ) . The final reduced spectra provide therefore usable coverage over 0.97 0.97 – 1.89 ​ μ 1.89\,\mu m, 1.70 1.70 – 4.00 ​ μ 4.00\,\mu m, and 1.66 1.66 – 2.97 ​ μ 2.97\,\mu m, respectively. G140M contains the rest-UV and blue rest-optical lines, G235M includes H ​ β {\rm H}\beta , [O iii ], and recovers the complete H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha +[N ii ] complex, while G235H provides higher-resolution coverage of H ​ β {\rm H}\beta and [O iii ] but does not cover H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha for this target (due to the detector gap).

sections.heading: 2.2 HST and JWST imaging
sections.text: The imaging data were retrieved from the version-7 mosaics assembled by the Dawn JWST Archive (DJA; Valentino et al. 2023 ; Brammer et al. 2025 ) . These mosaics combine all publicly available exposures at the target position on a common astrometric grid; the photometry used in this work is measured directly from the science and inverse-variance images. The principal broad-band NIRCam coverage ( Rieke et al., 2023 ) comes from PRIMER (PID 1837; Dunlop et al. 2021 ) and COSMOS-Web (PID 1727; Casey et al. 2023 ), with additional imaging from Blue Jay (PID 1810; Belli et al. 2026 ), COSMOS-3D (PID 5893), and MINERVA (PID 7814; Muzzin et al. 2025 ). Together these data provide NIRCam imaging from F090W to F460M. The DJA products also include archival HST/WFC3 and ACS imaging from F336W to F160W in the COSMOS field ( Scoville et al., 2007 ; Grogin et al., 2011 ; Koekemoer et al., 2011 ) , and MIRI imaging ( Wright et al., 2023 ) in F770W, F1000W, F1280W, F1500W, F1800W, and F2100W. Section 4 describes the image-level quality control, PSF treatment, aperture measurements, and the subset adopted for stellar-population fitting. Figure 1 shows the NIRCam imaging and NIRSpec/MSA footprint for MARTA 3887, with the target located in the central shutter and the three-point nodding pattern sampling five effective shutter positions on the sky. The native RGB image (panel (a)) emphasizes small-scale morphology, while the F444W-PSF-matched rendering (panel (b)) enables a consistent comparison of the light distribution across bands, albeit at reduced angular resolution. NIRCam imaging depicts MARTA 3887 as a multi-component system, with two knots of comparable brightness intercepted by the MSA spectroscopic aperture, and a fainter, southern knot outside of it; such a three-component nature is better seen at the highest resolution of short wavelength filters, as highlighted by the F150W-view of the system shown in panel (c) of Figure 1 (see also Sect. 4.1 and the full list of imaging cutouts in Appendix D.1 ). We note that, at the MSA slit orientation, the bright clumps have overlapping spatial profiles in the extracted NIRSpec spectra, and we therefore treat the one-dimensional spectrum as an integrated measurement of the two.

sections.heading: 2.3 Archival VLT/MUSE spectroscopy
sections.text: MARTA 3887 lies within the public MUSE-Wide pointing candels-cosmos-16 ( Bacon et al., 2010 ; Herenz et al., 2017 ; Urrutia et al., 2019 ) . We retrieved the reduced datacube from the ESO Science Archive (programme 097.A-0160(A), dataset ADP.2017-06-19T11:53:53.311). The fiducial full-depth cube combines two independently reduced observing stacks with different seeing. It has an effective on-source exposure time of 3867 s and covers 4749.5 4749.5 – 9349.5 9349.5 Å with a spectral sampling of 1.25 Å pixel -1 and a spatial sampling of 0.2 ′′ 0.2^{\prime\prime} pixel -1 . We use the full-depth cube for all fiducial measurements and the two constituent stacks only for robustness tests described in Appendix E . At the redshift of MARTA 3887 this range contains Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha and the principal rest-UV emission lines (which are, however, undetected, see Appendix E ). The astrometric correction and data processing of the MUSE datacube are outlined in Appendix E , while spectral extraction and spatial analysis of the Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission are discussed in Sect. 5 . We note that no other rest-UV line beyond Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha is robustly detected in the MUSE datacube; the apparent He II λ ​ 1640 \lambda 1640 feature is identified as a sky-subtraction residual through the independent-exposure tests described in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 3.1 Broad H α \alpha
sections.text: We fit the rest-frame λ ≃ 6450 \lambda\simeq 6450 – 6750 6750 Å region of the G235M spectrum using a local linear continuum and Gaussian emission-line components. Narrow H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha , [N ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 6548 , 6584 \lambda\lambda 6548,6584 , and [S ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 6718 , 6732 \lambda\lambda 6718,6732 share a common velocity and intrinsic dispersion; the [N ii ] doublet ratio is fixed to its atomic value. A second Gaussian is included to model any broad component for the (permitted) H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission. All components are convolved with the NIRSpec LSF before comparison with the data. The fit in Fig. 2 detects a broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component with fiducial flux F H ​ α , b = 1.69 × 10 − 18 ​ erg ​ s − 1 ​ cm − 2 F_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1.69\times 10^{-18}\ {\rm erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}} , luminosity L H ​ α , b = 2.35 × 10 41 L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=2.35\times 10^{41} erg s -1 , and intrinsic FWHM H ​ α , b ≃ 1270 {\rm FWHM}_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}\simeq 1270 km s -1 . Adopting the reference best fit as the fiducial central value, bootstrap refits give F H ​ α , b = 1.69 − 0.19 + 0.26 × 10 − 18 F_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1.69^{+0.26}_{-0.19}\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 and FWHM H ​ α , b = 1270 − 250 + 260 {\rm FWHM}_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1270^{+260}_{-250} km s -1 . The broad model is preferred to a narrow-only model by the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC; lower values are preferred), with Δ ​ BIC = − 46.8 \Delta{\rm BIC}=-46.8 . Figure 2: Fiducial fit to the H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha +[N ii ] complex in the NIRSpec/G235M spectrum. Narrow permitted and forbidden components share a common kinematic model, while broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha is fitted independently. All line components are convolved with the instrumental LSF. The top panel shows the 2-d spectrum, where each pixel is colour coded by signal-to-noise ratio. The second panel shows the extracted 1-d spectrum, with the best-fit model and individual components highlighted; the inset panel adopts a log-scale on the y y axis to highlight the broad component. The third panel shows the spectrum after subtracting only the continuum and narrow-line model, together with the inferred broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component; the bottom panel shows the residuals to the complete model. The detection of the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component remains robust against variation in the local continuum and narrow-line assumptions, is recovered in injection–recovery experiments, and is not produced at comparable significance in null trials. The two-dimensional G235M spectrum shows the spatially tilted narrow-line trace expected for a resolved source, with the line centroid shifting slightly along the spatial direction; collapsing this trace cannot reproduce the wavelength extent of the broad component. We additionally test whether blending among intermediate-width H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha and both [N ii ] lines, all sharing the [O iii ] non-core kinematics measured below, can account for the broad base, finding that it cannot replace the broad component. This test is fully described in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 3.2 H β \beta and [O iii ] constraints on the broad component
sections.text: We next fit only the H ​ β {\rm H}\beta +[O iii ] complex in G235M and G235H, without including the H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha region in the likelihood. The two gratings are fitted simultaneously with unite ( Hviding, 2025 ) , a package for the joint forward modeling of spectra from multiple gratings which includes a proper treatment of the LSFs and a relative flux-calibration nuisance parameter; in our model, we specifically assume shared narrow-line kinematics among the lines, while also including an ‘intermediate-width’ [O iii ] component to capture any faint non-core emission. We assume for each grating the LSF for a uniformly illuminated slit ( Jakobsen et al., 2022 ) , and allow a shared multiplicative correction factor to account for any deviation from the nominal resolving power; the fit prefers R scale = 1.086 ± 0.007 R_{\rm scale}=1.086\pm 0.007 for the G235M+G235H fit. Relative to a narrow-core-only model, including the intermediate [O iii ] component improves the fit by Δ ​ BIC = − 19.4 \Delta{\rm BIC}=-19.4 . Such a component has FWHM = 299 − 32 + 36 {\rm FWHM}=299^{+36}_{-32} km s -1 and Δ ​ v = − 61 − 35 + 21 \Delta v=-61^{+21}_{-35} km s -1 relative to the systemic redshift, and contributes at both wavelengths of the [O iii ] doublet (Fig. 3 ). Its width, however, is clearly distinct from that of the ≃ 1270 \simeq 1270 km s -1 component detected beneath H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha . We treat it as a phenomenological non-core component: while its modest blueshift is compatible with a low-velocity ionized-gas outflow, we note that unresolved kinematic structure within the clumpy source or residual mismatch between the true LSF and the uniformly illuminated-slit prescription could also contribute to the overall line profile. To further test for faint counterparts of the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha , we performed another fit in which we introduce Gaussian templates for broad H ​ β {\rm H}\beta and [O iii ] whose integrated fluxes are allowed to be either positive or negative. 2 2 2 Allowing signed amplitudes prevents a weak component from being biased positive by an imposed non-negative boundary. Each broad template is assigned an H α \alpha -informed truncated-Gaussian FWHM prior centred at 1270 km s -1 , with a standard deviation of 250 km s -1 and limits of 700–2200 km s -1 , together with a uniform − 200 < Δ ​ v < + 200 -200<\Delta v<+200 km s -1 velocity prior. When broad H β \beta and broad [O iii ] are included simultaneously, they share the same velocity and width. The corresponding 95th-percentile templates are overplotted across the full H ​ β {\rm H}\beta +[O iii ] complex in Fig. 3 . Adding these components gives Δ ​ BIC = + 11.4 \Delta{\rm BIC}=+11.4 , + 2.2 +2.2 , and + 1.8 +1.8 , respectively. Their small positive median amplitudes therefore do not compensate for the additional model parameters, and none is included in the fiducial H ​ β {\rm H}\beta +[O iii ] model. The model-conditional 95% limits are F H ​ β , b < 7.3 × 10 − 19 ​ erg ​ s − 1 ​ cm − 2 F_{{\rm H}\beta,{\rm b}}<7.3\times 10^{-19}\ {\rm erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}} and F [ O ​ III ] ​ 5007 , b < 9.4 × 10 − 19 ​ erg ​ s − 1 ​ cm − 2 F_{[\mathrm{O\,III}]5007,{\rm b}}<9.4\times 10^{-19}\ {\rm erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}} , with F [ O ​ III ] ​ 5007 , b / F [ O ​ III ] ​ 5007 , n < 0.036 F_{[\mathrm{O\,III}]5007,{\rm b}}/F_{[\mathrm{O\,III}]5007,{\rm n}}<0.036 . For an intrinsic broad-line decrement H ​ α / H ​ β = 3.1 {\rm H}\alpha/{\rm H}\beta=3.1 , the fiducial broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux predicts instead F H ​ β , b = 5.4 × 10 − 19 ​ erg ​ s − 1 ​ cm − 2 F_{{\rm H}\beta,{\rm b}}=5.4\times 10^{-19}\ {\rm erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}} , below the 95% limit: thus, the data neither require nor exclude the presence of a broad H ​ β {\rm H}\beta counterpart. Because the broad-line amplitudes remain weak, their posteriors depend on the adopted kinematic constraints. After marginalizing over the H α \alpha -informed width prior and the uniform − 200 < Δ ​ v < + 200 -200<\Delta v<+200 km s -1 prior adopted above, the broad-H β \beta limit provides no positive lower bound on A V , broad A_{V,{\rm broad}} . Fitting runs in which the broad-line kinematics are fixed or more tightly constrained yield formally stronger though explicitly prior-conditional limits. We therefore treat the broad H β \beta only as an upper limit and apply no extinction correction to the broad H α \alpha luminosity. Figure 3: Joint G235M (left) and G235H (right) fits to the full H ​ β {\rm H}\beta +[O iii ] complex. Red curves show the best-fit narrow+intermediate model. Solid blue and purple curves show the narrow components and the intermediate [O iii ] component included in the best-fit model. The dash-dotted orange curve is the broad- H ​ β {\rm H}\beta template normalized to the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux for H ​ α / H ​ β = 3.1 {\rm H}\alpha/{\rm H}\beta=3.1 ; it falls below the dashed teal 95% broad- H ​ β {\rm H}\beta test limit. The magenta dotted curve shows the 95th-percentile broad [O iii ] test template. The broad templates are not selected by BIC and are not included in the fiducial model; a symmetric-logarithmic flux scale is chosen here to highlight the inferred upper limits on their contribution. Lower panels show residuals in units of the rescaled uncertainty.

sections.heading: 3.3 Analysis of the narrow-line spectrum
sections.text: We fit 3 3 3 Wavelengths adopted in the analysis are vacuum wavelengths; a few conventional shorthand labels retained throughout the paper (for example, [O iii ] λ ​ 5007 \lambda 5007 ) assume air wavelengths but refer to the same transitions. the full narrow-line spectrum with a separate, LSF-convolved fit that combines G140M, G235M, and G235H. Non-resonant lines share a common intrinsic narrow-line velocity and width, while the Mg II λ ​ λ ​ 2796 , 2803 \lambda\lambda 2796,2803 doublet has independent kinematics because resonant scatter can shift and broaden its emergent profile. The [O iii ] doublet retains the intermediate component selected in the dedicated fitting described above, while neither H ​ β {\rm H}\beta nor [O iii ] contain any broad component in this fit. Each line complex has its underlying continuum modeled in simple linear form, and we include both a multiplicative factor to account for relative flux-calibration offsets between different gratings as well as a correction factor to model variations from the assumed LSF for a uniformly illuminated slit. Figure 4 shows the result of the fit. The shared narrow component has FWHM = 153 ± 3 {\rm FWHM}=153\pm 3 km s -1 and defines the systemic redshift adopted throughout this work, z sys = 3.76937 ± 0.00001 z_{\rm sys}=3.76937\pm 0.00001 (16th–84th percentile interval). The formal ≃ 3 \simeq 3 km s -1 difference between its centroid and the initial redshift used to initialize the fit is negligible at the NIRSpec resolution. The dedicated G235M fit also gives a formal 4.4 ​ σ 4.4\sigma detection of [Ar iii ] λ ​ 7138 \lambda 7138 . Because this wavelength lies close to the onset of the second-order-contaminated region, we report its flux but do not use it in the physical-condition or photoionization fits. The complete set of measured fluxes, posterior uncertainties, and adopted upper limits is reported in Table F . Figure 4: Narrow-line fitting across the three available grating spectra. The panels show the principal rest-UV and optical line complexes in G140M (green), G235M (blue), and G235H (red). Solid coloured curves are the best-fit LSF-convolved models, and dashed curves isolate the line components for marginally resolved doublets.

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Density, temperature, and nebular attenuation
sections.text: We infer the electron temperature, low-ionization electron density, and nebular attenuation jointly rather than in a sequence of independent calculations. The likelihood combines the posterior flux vectors and covariances of the four Balmer lines, [O iii ] λ ​ 4363 \lambda 4363 and λ ​ 5008 \lambda 5008 , the G235H [O ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 3727 , 3729 \lambda\lambda 3727,3729 doublet, and [S ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 6716 , 6731 \lambda\lambda 6716,6731 . We compare these flux vectors directly with the corresponding PyNeb emissivities ( Luridiana et al., 2015 ) , profiling over an independent non-negative normalization for each line family. This avoids constructing Gaussian approximations to ratios involving marginally detected lines. For O + , we adopt transition probabilities from Zeippen (1982) ; Wiese et al. (1996) and effective collision strengths from Kisielius et al. (2009) ; for O ++ , transition probabilities from Froese Fischer & Tachiev (2004) ; Storey & Zeippen (2000) and collision strengths from Storey et al. (2014) ; and for S + , transition probabilities from Rynkun et al. (2019) and collision strengths from Tayal & Zatsarinny (2010) . The H i recombination emissivities are from Storey & Hummer (1995) . The Balmer emissivities are evaluated at the sampled temperature and density and attenuated with the Cardelli et al. (1989) curve with R V = 3.1 R_{V}=3.1 . The [O iii ] λ ​ 4363 / λ ​ 5008 \lambda 4363/\lambda 5008 ratio constrains T 3 ≡ T e ​ ( O ​ III ) T_{3}\equiv T_{\rm e}({\rm O\,III}) , while [O ii ] and [S ii ] are assigned a common representative density for the low-ionization gas. Because [O ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 7320 , 7330 \lambda\lambda 7320,7330 is not detected, T 2 ≡ T e ​ ( O ​ II ) T_{2}\equiv T_{\rm e}({\rm O\,II}) is linked to T 3 T_{3} through the empirical relation of Cataldi et al. (2025) , including its intrinsic uncertainty. The ionic abundances are sampled simultaneously and are discussed in Sect. 3.3.4 . The G235H spectrum gives F 3729 / F 3727 = 1.19 − 0.23 + 0.33 F_{3729}/F_{3727}=1.19^{+0.33}_{-0.23} . The [S ii ] ratio, F 6716 / F 6731 = 0.51 − 0.25 + 0.26 F_{6716}/F_{6731}=0.51^{+0.26}_{-0.25} , nominally favours a higher density, although the weaker λ ​ 6716 \lambda 6716 component is detected at only S / N = 2.1 {\rm S/N}=2.1 . Allowing the two ions to have independent densities improves the fit by Δ ​ χ 2 = 4.2 \Delta\chi^{2}=4.2 relative to the common-density model, corresponding to only a ≃ 2 ​ σ \simeq 2\sigma tension. We therefore retain the common-density description while accounting for the full, non-Gaussian density posterior. The joint inference gives T 3 = 18,140 − 710 + 770 ​ K , n e = 310 − 300 + 600 ​ cm − 3 , T_{3}=18{,}140^{+770}_{-710}\ {\rm K},\qquad n_{\rm e}=310^{+600}_{-300}\ {\rm cm^{-3}}, and E ​ ( B − V ) neb = 0.054 ± 0.013 E(B-V)_{\rm neb}=0.054\pm 0.013 . The density posterior has a long tail towards the low-density limit and a one-sided 95% upper bound of n e < 1.5 × 10 3 n_{\rm e}<1.5\times 10^{3} cm -3 . The attenuation constraint is informed jointly by all four Balmer lines: H α \alpha comes from the dedicated local fit, whereas H γ \gamma /H β \beta and H δ \delta /H β \beta provide substantial leverage towards the fitted positive value. The inferred attenuation remains small under the adopted foreground-screen model and temperature-dependent Case-B emissivities. Alternative optical attenuation curves change the relevant corrected ratios by amounts well below their measurement uncertainties. Figure 5 shows the marginalized posterior distributions and covariances, together with the line ratios predicted by the posterior model. All principal ratios are reproduced within their uncertainties, apart from the mild tension associated with the marginal [S ii ] λ ​ 6716 \lambda 6716 measurement. Figure 5: Joint constraints on the physical conditions and ionic abundances of the narrow-line gas. The upper corner plot shows the marginalized posterior distributions and covariances of T 3 T_{3} , n e n_{\rm e} , E ​ ( B − V ) neb E(B-V)_{\rm neb} , O + /H + , and O ++ /H + . Contours enclose 68% and 95% credible regions. The lower panel compares the measured line ratios with those predicted by the posterior model. The [O ii ] density ratio is measured from G235H, whereas the remaining fluxes come from the joint narrow-line fitting of all available gratings (Sect. 3.3 ). The mild discrepancy for [S ii ] reflects the ≃ 2 ​ σ \simeq 2\sigma tension between the [O ii ] and [S ii ] density constraints and the low-S/N ( 2.1 2.1 ) detection of [S ii ] λ ​ 6716 \lambda 6716 .

sections.heading: 3.3.2 Constraints on high-ionization and high-density gas
sections.text: The [Ne iv ] λ ​ λ ​ 2422 , 2425 \lambda\lambda 2422,2425 doublet probes a more highly ionized phase than [O ii ] and [S ii ] and is therefore not included in the common-density inference above. In the joint spectral fit, λ ​ 2425 \lambda 2425 is detected at 3.65 ​ σ 3.65\sigma , whereas λ ​ 2422 \lambda 2422 is not individually detected ( 0.87 ​ σ 0.87\sigma ; P [ F 2422 > 0 ] = 0.81 P[F_{2422}>0]=0.81 ). The resulting posterior gives a one-sided 95% upper limit F 2422 / F 2425 < 0.92 F_{2422}/F_{2425}<0.92 . We constrain the density from the signed two-line flux vector rather than from a ratio between a detection and an upper limit. At each trial density, the PyNeb doublet ratio is fixed and a non-negative common normalization is fitted to both transitions, while positive and negative spectral fluctuations are retained in the likelihood. Marginalizing over the T 3 T_{3} posterior gives n e ​ ( Ne 3 + ) < 9.5 × 10 3 n_{\rm e}({\rm Ne^{3+}})<9.5\times 10^{3} cm -3 at 95% confidence; the limit varies by less than 2% across the allowed temperature range. Figure 6 compares this constraint directly with the individual low-ionization diagnostics. For each ion, the central curve is evaluated at the median of the relevant temperature posterior, while the shaded band spans its 16th–84th percentiles: T 2 T_{2} for [O ii ] and [S ii ], and T 3 T_{3} for [Ne iv ]. The [Ne iv ] constraint disfavors a very dense n e ≳ 10 4 n_{\rm e}\gtrsim 10^{4} cm -3 high-ionization component but remains compatible with a moderate-density narrow-line region. Conversely, the low-ionization density inferred above is typical of high-redshift H ii regions ( Sanders et al., 2016 ; Isobe et al., 2023 ; Topping et al., 2025 , e.g.) , but also overlaps the lower-density range of AGN narrow-line regions ( Zhang et al., 2013 ) . The density measurements alone therefore do not discriminate between stellar and AGN excitation. Figure 6: Electron-density constraints from gas at different ionization stages. The curves show the profile likelihoods obtained from the signed flux vectors and posterior covariances of [O ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 3727 , 3729 \lambda\lambda 3727,3729 in G235H (blue), [S ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 6716 , 6731 \lambda\lambda 6716,6731 in G235M (green), and [Ne iv ] λ ​ λ ​ 2422 , 2425 \lambda\lambda 2422,2425 in G140M (red), profiling independently over their normalizations. Central curves use the median T 2 T_{2} or T 3 T_{3} , with shaded bands propagating the corresponding 16th–84th percentile temperature range. The horizontal dashed line marks the one-sided 95% threshold ( Δ ​ χ 2 = 2.71 \Delta\chi^{2}=2.71 ); the bounds are n e ​ ( O + ) < 1.1 × 10 3 n_{\rm e}({\rm O^{+}})<1.1\times 10^{3} , n e ​ ( S + ) > 8.7 × 10 2 n_{\rm e}({\rm S^{+}})>8.7\times 10^{2} , and n e ​ ( Ne 3 + ) < 9.5 × 10 3 n_{\rm e}({\rm Ne^{3+}})<9.5\times 10^{3} cm -3 . The [S ii ] constraint is tentative because λ ​ 6716 \lambda 6716 is not individually detected above 3 ​ σ 3\sigma .

sections.heading: 3.3.3 Diagnostic diagrams and ionization source
sections.text: We here investigate the position of MARTA 3887 onto classical emission-line-ratio diagnostic diagrams which are commonly adopted to discriminate the dominant source of the ionizing spectrum. Specifically, we define N2 = [ N ​ II ] ​ λ ​ 6585 / H ​ α \mathrm{N2}=[\mathrm{N\,II}]\lambda 6585/{\rm H}\alpha , S2 = ( [ S ​ II ] ​ λ ​ 6716 + [ S ​ II ] ​ λ ​ 6731 ) / H ​ α \mathrm{S2}=([\mathrm{S\,II}]\lambda 6716+[\mathrm{S\,II}]\lambda 6731)/{\rm H}\alpha , and O1 = [ O ​ I ] ​ λ ​ 6300 / H ​ α \mathrm{O1}=[\mathrm{O\,I}]\lambda 6300/{\rm H}\alpha for the three classical BPT/VO87 panels ( Baldwin et al., 1981 ; Veilleux & Osterbrock, 1987 ) . We further define R 3 = [ O ​ III ] ​ λ ​ 5008 / H ​ β R_{3}=[\mathrm{O\,III}]\lambda 5008/{\rm H}\beta , O32 = [ O ​ III ] ​ λ ​ 5008 / ( [ O ​ II ] ​ λ ​ λ ​ 3727 , 3729 ) \mathrm{O32}=[\mathrm{O\,III}]\lambda 5008/([\mathrm{O\,II}]\lambda\lambda 3727,3729) , R 23 = ( [ O ​ II ] ​ λ ​ λ ​ 3727 , 3729 + [ O ​ III ] ​ λ ​ λ ​ 4960 , 5008 ) / H ​ β R_{23}=([\mathrm{O\,II}]\lambda\lambda 3727,3729+[\mathrm{O\,III}]\lambda\lambda 4960,5008)/{\rm H}\beta , Ne3O2 = [ Ne ​ III ] ​ λ ​ 3870 / [ O ​ II ] ​ λ ​ λ ​ 3727 , 3729 \mathrm{Ne3O2}=[\mathrm{Ne\,III}]\lambda 3870/[\mathrm{O\,II}]\lambda\lambda 3727,3729 , O3Hg = [ O ​ III ] ​ λ ​ 4363 / H ​ γ \mathrm{O3Hg}=[\mathrm{O\,III}]\lambda 4363/\mathrm{H}\gamma , and Ne4Hb = ( [ Ne ​ IV ] ​ λ ​ 2422 + [ Ne ​ IV ] ​ λ ​ 2425 ) / H ​ β \mathrm{Ne4Hb}=([\mathrm{Ne\,IV}]\lambda 2422+[\mathrm{Ne\,IV}]\lambda 2425)/{\rm H}\beta . [N ii ] and [O i ] λ ​ 6300 \lambda 6300 are undetected and are treated as 3 ​ σ 3\sigma upper limits, giving log ⁡ ( [ N ​ II ] / H ​ α ) < − 1.76 \log([\mathrm{N\,II}]/{\rm H}\alpha)<-1.76 and log ⁡ ( [ O ​ I ] / H ​ α ) < − 1.62 \log([\mathrm{O\,I}]/{\rm H}\alpha)<-1.62 . Figure 7 compares these ratios with local SDSS DR7 galaxies ( Abazajian et al., 2009 ) , using emission-line measurements from the MPA–JHU catalogue ( Brinchmann et al., 2004 ; Tremonti et al., 2004 ) . They are separated a priori into star-forming and AGN/composite populations using their position relative to the Kauffmann et al. (2003) demarcation in the [N ii ]-BPT diagram. The same classification is retained in all other optical-line-based panels. The JADES comparison sample is drawn from DR4 ( Curtis-Lake et al., 2026 ; Scholtz et al., 2026 ; Eisenstein et al., 2023 ) . Standard diagnostic boundaries ( Kauffmann et al., 2003 ; Kewley et al., 2001 ; Kewley et al., 2006 ; Kewley et al., 2013 ) and the JADES DR4 emission-line sample are also shown, with Type 1 AGN identified in Juodžbalis et al. (2026) highlighted. The measured log ⁡ O32 = 1.08 \log\mathrm{O32}=1.08 , log ⁡ R 3 = 0.77 \log R_{3}=0.77 , log ⁡ R 23 = 0.92 \log R_{23}=0.92 , and log ⁡ Ne3O2 = − 0.04 \log\mathrm{Ne3O2}=-0.04 are characteristic of a high-ionization, low-metallicity galaxy, placing MARTA 3887 at the extreme end of the star-forming sequence in the classical BPT and R 23 R_{23} –O32 diagrams ( Strom et al., 2017 , e.g.) . Its narrow-line ratios are therefore compatible with metal-poor, hard stellar ionizing spectra, and do not independently require an AGN contribution. In the diagnostic diagram proposed by Mazzolari et al. (2024) , which leverages the detection of the auroral line [O iii ] λ ​ 4363 \lambda 4363 , ID 3887 lies close to, or nominally just above, the proposed demarcation between AGN and galaxies hosting either star formation, an AGN, or both (panel e of Fig. 7 ), in line with several other similar JADES type 1 AGN candidates. Given the measurement uncertainty, proximity to the boundaries, and inferred low metallicity, we treat this primarily as further evidence for a hard stellar ionizing spectrum, while acknowledging the potential for a non-negligible AGN contribution. The [Ne iv ] λ ​ λ ​ 2422 , 2425 \lambda\lambda 2422,2425 detection ( 3.6 ​ σ 3.6\sigma ) provides an additional probe of the ionizing spectrum. Although [Ne iv ] is often associated with AGN photoionization at high redshift ( Nakajima & Maiolino, 2022 ; Cleri et al., 2023 ; Maiolino et al., 2024b , e.g.) , hard stellar spectra and stellar end products can also enhance high-ionization lines in metal-poor galaxies ( Shirazi & Brinchmann, 2012 ; Senchyna et al., 2017 ; Schaerer et al., 2019 ) . From the summed doublet flux we obtain log ⁡ ( [ Ne ​ IV ] / H ​ β ) = − 1.20 ± 0.12 \log([\mathrm{Ne\,IV}]/{\rm H}\beta)=-1.20\pm 0.12 and log ⁡ ( [ Ne ​ IV ] / [ Ne ​ III ] ) = − 0.84 ± 0.12 \log([\mathrm{Ne\,IV}]/[\mathrm{Ne\,III}])=-0.84\pm 0.12 , while a 3 ​ σ 3\sigma limit on [Ne v ] λ ​ 3426 \lambda 3426 gives log ⁡ ( [ Ne ​ V ] / [ Ne ​ IV ] ) < − 0.25 \log([\mathrm{Ne\,V}]/[\mathrm{Ne\,IV}])<-0.25 . The [Ne iv ]–Ne3O2 panel of Fig. 7 compares the detected ratio with the Gutkin et al. (2016) star-forming and Feltre et al. (2016) AGN narrow-line grids. MARTA 3887 can be reached by the star-forming grid, but mainly at a metallicity of Z ≃ 0.017 Z\simeq 0.017 –0.020 (i.e. approximately solar), substantially above the conditional ‘direct’ T e T_{\rm e} -based abundance (Sect. 3.3.4 ). Such a mismatch may descend from limitations of the single-zone photoionization models or effectively mark the requirement for an additional hard ionizing component. It should not, however, be read as a direct inconsistency: an AGN contribution would also invalidate some of the assumptions used to convert the measured temperatures and ionic abundances into a total O/H in classical H ii regions. The low significance of the [Ne iv ] detection and the absence of [Ne v ] emission though suggest only a mild AGN contribution to the narrow-line spectrum, while a proper quantitative decomposition remains difficult: we test this with dedicated photoionization modeling at the end of Sect. 3.3.4 ). sections.heading: 3.3.4 Gas-phase metallicity
sections.text: The joint inference described in Sect. 3.3.1 also samples the ionic abundances together with T 3 T_{3} , T 2 T_{2} , n e n_{\rm e} , and E ​ ( B − V ) neb E(B-V)_{\rm neb} . At each posterior step, O + /H + is derived from the [O ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 3727 , 3729 \lambda\lambda 3727,3729 /H β \beta ratio using the sampled T 2 T_{2} and low-ionization density. O ++ /H + is derived from [O iii ] λ ​ 5008 \lambda 5008 /H β \beta using the sampled T 3 T_{3} and n e = 10 3 n_{\rm e}=10^{3} cm -3 for the O ++ zone. The latter is a representative value consistent with the [Ne iv ] limit; the [O iii ] emissivities are insensitive to density over the allowed range. The resulting low-ionization temperature is T 2 = 14,610 − 740 + 750 T_{2}=14{,}610^{+750}_{-740} K, where the uncertainty includes the scatter of the adopted T 2 T_{2} – T 3 T_{3} relation. Summing the ionic abundances, O / H = O + / H + + O + ⁣ + / H + \mathrm{O/H}=\mathrm{O^{+}/H^{+}}+\mathrm{O^{++}/H^{+}} , gives 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) = 7.68 ± 0.04 . 12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm 0.04. The posterior covariance among temperature, density, attenuation, and line fluxes is included directly in this uncertainty. Approximately 91% of the inferred oxygen abundance is in O ++ , so the result is only weakly sensitive to the adopted low-ionization density and T 2 T_{2} – T 3 T_{3} relation. The measurement of T 3 T_{3} from [O iii ] λ ​ 4363 / λ ​ 5008 \lambda 4363/\lambda 5008 , and the corresponding O ++ /H + ionic abundance, do not require an assumption about the shape of the stellar ionizing spectrum. Interpreting the ionic sum as the total oxygen abundance is instead conditional on stellar-dominated narrow-line excitation, the adopted two-zone temperature structure, and a negligible contribution from higher oxygen ionization stages. The integrated spectrum may also combine regions with different temperatures, densities, and ionizing sources, in which case the inferred quantities are emissivity-weighted effective values. We assess these systematics below.

sections.heading: Sensitivity to a possible AGN contribution
sections.text: Because the detection of broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission (Sect. 3.1 ) suggests the presence of an accreting black hole in the system (Sect. 6.1 ), we investigate whether AGN-powered emission could alter the gas-phase metallicity inference described above. In fact, if an AGN contributes significantly to the narrow-line ionization, its harder continuum can alter the temperature stratification relative to what is assumed for classical H ii regions and star-forming galaxies; while photoionization equilibrium may still hold, converting the measured temperatures and ionic abundances into a ‘total’ O/H would hence require stellar-plus-AGN models that jointly constrain the incident SED, ionization parameter, density, dust, and abundance patterns ( Osterbrock & Ferland, 2006 ; Feltre et al., 2016 , e.g.) . Furthermore, this would place a non-negligible fraction of oxygen in O 3 + \mathrm{O^{3+}} (in which case an ionization-correction factor would be required and the ionic sum of O + \mathrm{O^{+}} and O + ⁣ + \mathrm{O^{++}} would not represent the total oxygen abundance). However, we detect no significant Si iv +O iv ] λ ​ 1400 \lambda 1400 emission in the (shallow) MUSE spectrum, with a 3 ​ σ 3\sigma flux limit of 3.9 × 10 − 18 3.9\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 for the blended complex, nor secure narrow He ii λ ​ 4686 \lambda 4686 emission in the NIRSpec spectrum. We therefore find no direct evidence that O 3 + \mathrm{O^{3+}} contributes substantially and apply no additional ionization correction, while noting that such non-detections do not provide a stringent quantitative limit on O 3 + / O \mathrm{O^{3+}/O} . To test the sensitivity to the ionizing spectrum directly, we fitted the MARTA 3887 narrow-line fluxes with the multi-cloud photoionization framework homerun ( Marconi et al., 2024 ; Moreschini et al., 2026 ) , adopting either purely stellar or composite stellar+AGN continua. The model construction and the line-by-line decomposition of the composite solution are presented in Appendix C . Both model families reproduce the observed line ratios within the adopted model tolerance; their objective-function values provide a relative ranking within each model family, rather than a formal χ 2 \chi^{2} preference between them. We note however that the stellar-only fit reproduces [Ne iv ] only through a substantial contribution from gas with log ⁡ U > − 1 \log U>-1 , or through matter-bounded clouds as proposed by Moreschini et al. (2026) ; in the composite fit, the AGN-ionized component instead produces nearly all of the [Ne iv ] emission. The attenuation remains negligible in both model families. For the composite models, we impose a prior on f AGN ​ ( H ​ β ) ≤ 10 % f_{\rm AGN}({\rm H}\beta)\leq 10\% , motivated by the ionizing-photon budget inferred from broad H α \alpha under the preferred BLR interpretation (Sect. 6.1 ). Given the standard Cloudy ( Ferland et al., 2017 ) AGN continuum adopted by homerun , 4 4 4 The adopted SED has T BB = 10 5 T_{\rm BB}=10^{5} K, α uv = − 0.5 \alpha_{\rm uv}=-0.5 , α x = − 1 \alpha_{x}=-1 , and α ox = − 1.8 \alpha_{\rm ox}=-1.8 . It gives L ⁡ ( h ​ ν > 13.6 ​ eV ) / L bol ≃ 0.12 L(h\nu>13.6\,\mathrm{eV})/L_{\rm bol}\simeq 0.12 , a mean ionizing-photon energy of ≃ 1.7 \simeq 1.7 Ryd, and Q AGN ≃ 3.2 × 10 9 ​ ( L bol / erg ​ s − 1 ) Q_{\rm AGN}\simeq 3.2\times 10^{9}(L_{\rm bol}/{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}) s -1 . the broad-H α \alpha luminosity corresponds to Q AGN ≃ ( 1 CLOSE Q_{\rm AGN}\simeq(1 – OPEN 2 ) × 10 53 2)\times 10^{53} s -1 . The AGN can therefore power a fraction f AGN ​ ( H ​ β ) ≃ ( 0.04 CLOSE f_{\rm AGN}({\rm H}\beta)\simeq(0.04 – OPEN 0.09 ) ​ C NLR 0.09)C_{\rm NLR} of the narrow Balmer emission, where C NLR ≤ 1 C_{\rm NLR}\leq 1 is the narrow-line-region covering factor. A hotter accretion disc appropriate for a ∼ 10 6.5 ​ M ⊙ \sim 10^{6.5}\,M_{\odot} black hole can raise this estimate by up to a factor of ∼ 2.5 \sim 2.5 ; the 10% ceiling should therefore be regarded as a fiducial modeling prior rather than a strict physical upper limit. The best-fitting composite solution has f AGN ​ ( H ​ β ) = 9 % f_{\rm AGN}({\rm H}\beta)=9\% and reproduces all lines within 1 ​ σ 1\sigma , except [S ii ], which is reproduced within 1.5 ​ σ 1.5\sigma . The predicted, model-based oxygen abundance is 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) 12+\log({\rm O/H}) =7.79 for the stellar-only fit and 7.81 for the composite fit, a difference of only 0.02 0.02 dex. In the latter solution, the AGN component contributes ≃ 8 % \simeq 8\% and ≃ 13 % \simeq 13\% of [O iii ] λ ​ 5007 \lambda 5007 and λ ​ 4363 \lambda 4363 , respectively: removing these contributions changes T e ​ ( O ​ III ) T_{\rm e}({\rm O\,III}) and O ++ /H + for the stellar-photoionized gas by approximately − 500 -500 K and less than 0.03 dex. We note that the ∼ 0.13 \sim 0.13 dex offset between the composite homerun oxygen abundance and our fiducial, Te-based estimate persists even in the stellar-only scenario, showing that it is not driven by the inclusion of an AGN continuum but mostly reflects instead the sensitivity of the classical two-zone approach to unresolved density and ionization structures ( Moreschini et al., 2026 ) . As a final, illustrative sensitivity test, replacing the H ii -region T 2 T_{2} – T 3 T_{3} calibration with the NLR relation of Dors et al. (2020) 5 5 5 We note such a relation was calibrated for Type 2 AGN narrow-line regions and is mildly extrapolated here towards lower metallicity. gives T e ​ ( O ​ II ) ≃ 9200 T_{\rm e}({\rm O\,II})\simeq 9200 K and 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) ≃ 7.83 12+\log({\rm O/H})\simeq 7.83 , close to the homerun result. We hence retain 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) = 7.68 ± 0.04 12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm 0.04 as the fiducial, conditional H ii -region-like oxygen abundance estimate, and allow for an upward systematic of approximately 0.15 dex associated with the unresolved ionization structure; such an uncertainty, however, does not alter the classification of MARTA 3887 as a metal-poor galaxy, nor any of the conclusions of this paper.

sections.heading: 3.3.5 Mg II emission
sections.text: The Mg II λ ​ λ ​ 2796 , 2803 \lambda\lambda 2796,2803 doublet is detected in emission with an intrinsic FWHM = 195 − 90 + 62 {\rm FWHM}=195^{+62}_{-90} km s -1 and a centroid offset of + 35 − 13 + 13 +35^{+13}_{-13} km s -1 from systemic. No broad Mg II component is required, and the present spectrum shows no evidence for blueshifted Mg II absorption. The measured ratio, R MgII = F 2796 / F 2803 = 1.90 − 0.22 + 0.27 R_{\rm MgII}=F_{2796}/F_{2803}=1.90^{+0.27}_{-0.22} , is close to the optically thin value of two. In the idealized foreground-screen model, R MgII = 2 ​ exp ⁡ ( − τ 2803 ) R_{\rm MgII}=2\exp(-\tau_{2803}) ( Chisholm et al., 2020 ) , and the best-fit ratio corresponds to τ 2803 ≃ 0.05 \tau_{2803}\simeq 0.05 ; we note however that the uncertainty extends beyond the physical optically thin limit, and resonant scattering can redirect photons both into and out of the line of sight, hampering a proper quantitative estimate of the optical depth. The narrow profile rules out Mg II as an independent BLR virial-mass estimator and instead associates it with gas processed by the host ISM or narrow-line region. Emission without a detected blueshifted absorption trough does not select a unique origin: it can arise from intrinsically emitted low-optical-depth gas, resonant scattering, or an outflow viewed in an unfavourable geometry ( Erb et al., 2012 ; Martin et al., 2013 , e.g.) . Its doublet ratio is nevertheless consistent with low-optical-depth channels through which Ly α \alpha (Sect. 5 ) and LyC photons may escape, as found e.g. in Green Pea galaxies ( Henry et al., 2018 ; Chisholm et al., 2020 ) . However, in the presence of clumpy geometries the doublet ratio can remain close to two even when optically thick material covers part of the source, while dust and viewing angle alter the emergent fluxes; radiation-hydrodynamic calculations consequently find substantial scatter between Mg II and LyC escape ( Katz et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: 4.1 Morphology and photometry
sections.text: As shown already by Fig. 1 (as well as in the full cutouts of Fig. D1 in Appendix D.2 ), when observed in the rest-frame UV MARTA 3887 appears as constituted by two dominant knots separated by 0.161 0.161 – 0.167 ′′ 0.167^{\prime\prime} ( 1.17 1.17 – 1.22 1.22 proper kpc) and a fainter southern component 0.115 0.115 – 0.125 ′′ 0.125^{\prime\prime} ( 0.84 0.84 – 0.91 0.91 proper kpc) from the south-western knot. Their projected separations establish a multicomponent morphology but do not distinguish star-forming clumps from dynamically distinct merging units. PSF-convolved modelling favours three components in F115W–F200W, with the southern clump contributing 13–17% of the light. Figure 8 illustrates the result in F150W: adding the southern component removes the coherent residual below the two brighter knots and improves the fit by Δ ​ BIC = − 264 \Delta\mathrm{BIC}=-264 . The full multi-band modelling description and assumptions, together with the associated tests, are presented in Appendix D.2 . A forced decomposition at longer wavelengths suggests that the south-western component is redder than the north-eastern one, but becomes increasingly prior-dependent as the PSF broadens. In the following, we therefore adopt only the total, integrated photometry of the system for the purposes of SED-based inference. Figure 8: PSF-convolved morphological fit on the native F150W image. From left to right, the panels show the data, the two-component model and its residuals, and the three-component model and its residuals, expressed in units of the pixel uncertainty. The third component accounts for 16% of the fitted F150W light and removes the southern excess left by the two-component model. For the fiducial SED fitting we adopt a common 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture and apply filter-dependent STPSF encircled-energy corrections ( Perrin et al., 2014 ) . NIRCam fluxes are PSF-matched to the F460M reference PSF, whereas HST optical fluxes are retained in native images but measured in the same physical aperture. The HST F435W and F475W measurements are retained as signed flux constraints on the Lyman break, whereas the F336W non-detection is treated as an upper limit and also constrains direct LyC emission (Sect. 6.4 ). sections.heading: 4.2 SED fitting and sensitivity to different SFH priors
sections.text: We fit the integrated photometry with BAGPIPES ( Carnall et al., 2018 ) and sample the posterior with nautilus ( Lange, 2023 ) ; broad-band photometry is input without subtracting the narrow emission line fluxes, such that their contributions are predicted self-consistently by the BAGPIPES nebular module, and no spectroscopic line flux is supplied as a separate constraint (with the exception of H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha and F300M as described above). The redshift is fixed from the spectroscopy, and we adopt the BPASS v2.2.1 binary stellar-population models ( Stanway & Eldridge, 2018 ) with a imf135_300 broken-power-law IMF, i.e d ​ N / d ​ M ∝ M − 1.30 {\rm d}N/{\rm d}M\propto M^{-1.30} from 0.1 to 0.5 ​ M ⊙ 0.5\,M_{\odot} and ∝ M − 2.35 \propto M^{-2.35} from 0.5 to 300 ​ M ⊙ 300\,M_{\odot} . We use a six-bin non-parametric SFH: the logarithmic ratios of adjacent-bin SFRs follow a Student- t t continuity prior with scale 0.3, and we repeat the fit with scales 0.6 and 1.0 to test sensitivity to the regularization. The stellar metallicity has a log-uniform prior over 0.01 < Z / Z ⊙ < 0.3 0.01<Z/Z_{\odot}<0.3 . Dust follows a modified Charlot–Fall power law ( Charlot & Fall, 2000 ) , A λ ∝ λ − n A_{\lambda}\propto\lambda^{-n} , with A V A_{V} and n n fitted; stars younger than 10 Myr and nebular emission receive twice the diffuse-ISM attenuation. The resulting fit to the global host photometry is shown in Fig. 9 . The fiducial fit gives log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) = 8.16 − 0.10 + 0.09 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10} , log ⁡ ( M ⋆ , formed / M ⊙ ) = 8.22 − 0.10 + 0.11 \log(M_{\star,\rm formed}/M_{\odot})=8.22^{+0.11}_{-0.10} , and a BAGPIPES-reported 100-Myr-averaged SFR = 1.44 − 0.41 + 0.33 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 {\rm SFR}=1.44^{+0.33}_{-0.41}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} . The diffuse attenuation is A V = 0.021 − 0.012 + 0.037 A_{V}=0.021^{+0.037}_{-0.012} mag; the fixed birth-cloud factor therefore gives A V , young = 0.043 − 0.025 + 0.075 A_{V,{\rm young}}=0.043^{+0.075}_{-0.025} mag for stars younger than 10 Myr. Expressing the fitted Charlot–Fall curve as the corresponding colour excess, A B − A V A_{B}-A_{V} , gives E ​ ( B − V ) young = 0.012 − 0.005 + 0.008 E(B-V)_{\rm young}=0.012^{+0.008}_{-0.005} , lower than the independent Balmer-decrement result, E ​ ( B − V ) neb = 0.054 ± 0.013 E(B-V)_{\rm neb}=0.054\pm 0.013 (Sect. 3.3.1 ), although the two estimates remain consistent within approximately 3 ​ σ 3\sigma and assume different attenuation geometries and curves. The mass-weighted age is 70 − 51 + 180 70^{+180}_{-51} Myr. Broadening the continuity scale to 0.6 and 1.0 gives median surviving masses of 8.15 and 8.11 dex, respectively, but younger and more sharply rising median SFHs: the integrated stellar mass is thus comparatively stable within the regularized continuity family, whereas the detailed early SFH and the onset of the present burst remain prior-sensitive, as expected for non-parametric photometric reconstructions ( Leja et al., 2019 ) . Rising priors can be physically useful at high redshift ( Turner et al., 2025 ) , but we do not adopt one as the fiducial model because it would impose the desired early-time behaviour directly. An unregularized-SFH fit recovers a 0.46-dex lower stellar mass, but provides a poorer photometric fit ( Δ ​ χ 2 = 7.5 \Delta\chi^{2}=7.5 ; Appendix D.3 ). We retain the continuity result with scale=0.3 as the fiducial value and propagate this downward excursion as an asymmetric host-model systematic in Fig. 11 and the related discussion. From the fiducial posterior, the lookback times at which 10% and 50% of the final formed mass were already in place are t 10 = 92 − 61 + 891 ​ Myr t_{10}=92^{+891}_{-61}\ {\rm Myr} and t 50 = 18 − 5 + 8 ​ Myr t_{50}=18^{+8}_{-5}\ {\rm Myr} ; the long upper tail of t 10 t_{10} is relevant, as the data clearly identify a recent dominant episode but do not determine whether a low-level older component existed. In this sense, we also perform a ‘maximally-old stress test’, as described in Appendix D , limiting any hidden old component to M old , formed < 4.6 × 10 7 ​ M ⊙ M_{\rm old,formed}<4.6\times 10^{7}\,M_{\odot} at 95% posterior probability (Fig. D3 ). The fiducial BAGPIPES model contains stellar and nebular emission but no AGN continuum. We test for possible systematics on the stellar mass inference by fitting the photometry simultaneously with the same host model and an additional AGN power law, spanning − 1 ≤ α ν ≤ 0 -1\leq\alpha_{\nu}\leq 0 . The compact broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha contribution is first integrated through and subtracted from each filter —the only non-negligible corrections being in F277W and F356W— while the narrow nebular lines remain included self-consistently in the model. The data do not require a positive AGN component: the host+AGN fits have Δ ​ ln ⁡ 𝒵 = − 3.7 \Delta\ln\mathcal{Z}=-3.7 to − 3.4 -3.4 relative to the host-only fit, and the envelope over the range of adopted slopes gives an AGN fraction below 10.3% at rest-frame 5100 Å (95% posterior probability). The corresponding median stellar masses span 8.14 ≤ log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≤ 8.16 8.14\leq\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\leq 8.16 , i.e. offset only by − 0.05 -0.05 to − 0.02 -0.02 dex relative to the fiducial fit. We note that such constraints apply only to the emergent AGN continuum in the model and do not limit an intrinsic nuclear continuum that might be subject to independent attenuation.

sections.heading: 4.3 Aperture-matched H α \alpha star-formation rate
sections.text: The narrow H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha luminosity provides an independent tracer of star formation on a ≲ 10 \lesssim 10 Myr timescale, provided that its excitation is dominated by massive stars. To perform a meaningful comparison with the SED-based SFR estimate, we aperture-correct the measured H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux by mapping the NIRSpec point-source-calibrated narrow-line spectrum to the 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} -radius aperture used for the SED fitting. We define C ap ≡ F 0.5 ′′ / F NIRSpec , ps C_{\rm ap}\equiv F_{0.5^{\prime\prime}}/F_{\rm NIRSpec,ps} , where F NIRSpec , ps F_{\rm NIRSpec,ps} is the flux returned by the point-source-calibrated one-dimensional extraction. At the observed wavelength of H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha , F300M gives C ap = 1.76 C_{\rm ap}=1.76 , with a conservative range 1.64–2.10 that brackets the PSF-transfer and direct synthetic-photometry tests (Appendix A ). The resulting, ‘total’ narrow-line flux is F H ​ α , n = 2.28 × 10 − 17 F_{\rm H\alpha,n}=2.28\times 10^{-17} erg s -1 cm -2 , or L H ​ α , n = 3.18 × 10 42 L_{\rm H\alpha,n}=3.18\times 10^{42} erg s -1 before attenuation correction, which becomes 3.61 × 10 42 3.61\times 10^{42} erg s -1 assuming the joint Balmer-decrement constraint from Sect. 3.3.1 . To derive the H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha -based SFR, we use the high-redshift, sub-solar-metallicity conversion of Clarke et al. (2024) , also adopted by Khostovan et al. (2026) , log ⁡ ( SFR H ​ α M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 ) = log ⁡ ( L H ​ α erg ​ s − 1 ) − 41.59 \log\left(\frac{{\rm SFR}_{\rm H\alpha}}{M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}}\right)=\log\left(\frac{L_{\rm H\alpha}}{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}\right)-41.59 . This gives SFR H ​ α = 9.3 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 {\rm SFR}_{\rm H\alpha}=9.3\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} , with an aperture-mapping range of 8.6 8.6 – 11.1 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 11.1\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} and an additional ≃ 0.15 \simeq 0.15 -dex conversion systematic associated with the poorly constrained stellar iron abundance. The SED-based posterior gives SFR 0 − 10 ​ Myr = 5.42 − 0.52 + 0.77 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 {\rm SFR}_{0-10\,{\rm Myr}}=5.42^{+0.77}_{-0.52}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} and predicts an attenuated H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux of 1.98 − 0.18 + 0.19 × 10 − 17 1.98^{+0.19}_{-0.18}\times 10^{-17} erg s -1 cm -2 ; the aperture-matched observed flux is approximately 15% higher. The larger difference between SFR 0 − 10 ​ Myr {\rm SFR}_{0-10\,{\rm Myr}} and the narrow-H α \alpha estimate below also reflects the different BPASS and metal-poor H α \alpha –SFR conversions and their attenuation prescriptions. We therefore regard the two estimates as consistent within the calibration, aperture, and excitation systematics and the short-timescale variability expected for this bursty system.

sections.heading: 5 MUSE Ly α \alpha emission
sections.text: We here analyze VLT/MUSE observations (Sect. 2 ) of MARTA 3887, probing its rest-frame UV spectrum. After registering the MUSE WCS (see Appendix E ), clear emission is seen in the datacube at 0.037 ′′ 0.037^{\prime\prime} from the NIRCam position—consistent with the astrometric uncertainty—which we identify as Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha . The left-hand panel of Figure 10 shows the ‘pseudo narrow-band’ surface brightness map obtained by collapsing the datacube over the line, the r = 0.8 ′′ r=0.8^{\prime\prime} aperture maximizing the SNR and used to study the line profile, and the r = 1.4 ′′ r=1.4^{\prime\prime} aperture adopted to recover the total flux, as set by the curve of growth approaching its plateau (inset panel). The emission is spatially resolved and elongated. An elliptical-Gaussian fit gives an observed FWHM of 1.24 ′′ × 0.84 ′′ 1.24^{\prime\prime}\times 0.84^{\prime\prime} , compared with a 0.85 ′′ × 0.76 ′′ 0.85^{\prime\prime}\times 0.76^{\prime\prime} PSF, and a deconvolved FWHM of approximately 0.95 ′′ × 0.23 ′′ 0.95^{\prime\prime}\times 0.23^{\prime\prime} ( 6.9 × 1.7 6.9\times 1.7 proper kpc) at a major-axis position angle of ≃ 133 ∘ \simeq 133^{\circ} . The Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission encompasses the multiclump UV source, extends beyond it, and probes the inner ISM or CGM without isolating an individual knot. The measured deconvolved major-axis FWHM of ≃ 7 \simeq 7 proper kpc and the curve-of-growth plateau at ≃ 10 \simeq 10 proper kpc are comparable to the compact Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha haloes commonly detected around high-redshift star-forming galaxies ( Wisotzki et al., 2016 ; Leclercq et al., 2017 ; Kusakabe et al., 2022 ) . They are substantially smaller than the ∼ 50 \sim 50 – 100 100 proper-kpc nebulae routinely recovered around optically luminous quasars in MUSE surveys ( Borisova et al., 2016 ; Arrigoni Battaia et al., 2019 ; Lusso et al., 2019 ; Fossati et al., 2021 ) . This comparison is however purely descriptive, since both the ionizing luminosity and the surface-brightness sensitivity differ markedly between the samples; the present observations therefore do not exclude a fainter large-scale halo around MARTA 3887. The right-hand panel of Fig. 10 shows the extracted Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha profile and its best-fit. The line-profile models are convolved with the wavelength-dependent MUSE line-spread function measured by Bacon et al. (2017) ; at the observed Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha wavelength this corresponds to FWHM LSF = 2.69 {\rm FWHM}_{\rm LSF}=2.69 Å ( 139 139 km s -1 ). The total flux is F Ly ​ α = 9.97 × 10 − 17 F_{\rm Ly\alpha}=9.97\times 10^{-17} erg s -1 cm -2 , or L Ly ​ α = 1.39 × 10 43 L_{\rm Ly\alpha}=1.39\times 10^{43} erg s -1 . A two-sided Gaussian profile is preferred over a symmetric Gaussian by Δ ​ BIC asym − sym = − 36.4 \Delta{\rm BIC}_{\rm asym-sym}=-36.4 . The intrinsic FWHM is 245 − 22 + 21 245^{+21}_{-22} km s -1 , the peak offset is + 64 − 8 + 10 +64^{+10}_{-8} km s -1 with respect to the systemic redshift, and the red-to-blue width ratio is 2.85 − 0.46 + 0.43 2.85^{+0.43}_{-0.46} . Figure 10: Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission in the MUSE datacube. The left panel shows the continuum-subtracted narrow-band map, with the 0.8 ′′ 0.8^{\prime\prime} profile aperture in cyan and the 1.4 ′′ 1.4^{\prime\prime} total-flux aperture in green; the inset shows the corresponding curve of growth. The right panel shows the 0.8 ′′ 0.8^{\prime\prime} -extracted spectrum (maximizing the S/N) and the symmetric and two-sided-Gaussian fits, while the lower-right panel shows the normalized residuals to the latter. The spectrum is not sufficiently sensitive to robustly detect any unattenuated broad- Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha flux as predicted from the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha (Sect. 5 ). We use the aperture-corrected narrow H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux, F H ​ α , n ​ ( r < 0.5 ′′ ) = 2.28 × 10 − 17 F_{\rm H\alpha,n}(r<0.5^{\prime\prime})=2.28\times 10^{-17} erg s -1 cm -2 (Sect. 4.3 ), to infer a F Ly ​ α / F H ​ α , n = 4.38 F_{\rm Ly\alpha}/F_{\rm H\alpha,n}=4.38 ; this assumes that the non-resonant H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission is compact and enclosed by the 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture, while any additional extended H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission would lower the inferred escape fraction. The observed Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha flux is not dust-corrected: absorption by dust, enhanced by resonant scattering, is one of the losses that f esc Ly ​ α f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Ly\alpha} is intended to measure. The H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux is corrected because it provides the non-resonant estimate of the intrinsic recombination luminosity. Applying a foreground-screen correction to Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha would remove part of the attenuation being measured and would not capture its non-local resonant transfer. For Case B recombination at the measured gas temperature and density (Sect. 3.3.1 ), the intrinsic ratio is ( Ly ​ α / H ​ α ) int = 8.82 (\mathrm{Ly}\alpha/{\rm H}\alpha)_{\rm int}=8.82 . We therefore define f esc Ly ​ α = F obs ​ ( Ly ​ α ) / [ 8.82 ​ F int ​ ( H ​ α ) ] f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Ly\alpha}=F_{\rm obs}(\mathrm{Ly}\alpha)/[8.82\,F_{\rm int}({\rm H}\alpha)] , which gives f esc Ly ​ α ≃ 0.44 f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Ly\alpha}\simeq 0.44 with an allowed range 0.36–0.48 reflecting the conservative C ap C_{\rm ap} envelope for H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha aperture correction and the uncertainty on E ​ ( B − V ) neb E(B-V)_{\rm neb} . We note that the apertures remain imperfectly matched, as the MUSE Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha flux is integrated to r = 1.4 ′′ r=1.4^{\prime\prime} , whereas the H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha mapping is tied to the r = 0.5 ′′ r=0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture used in the SED fitting; furthermore, the relative MUSE/NIRSpec absolute calibration remains uncertain. Additional Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha production through fluorescence or collisional excitation would also bias this simple recombination-based estimate high. At face value, the measured escape fraction implies that a substantial fraction of the Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha photons produced by recombinations escape into the ≃ 10 \simeq 10 kpc aperture despite resonant scattering, consistent with a low effective dust opacity and low-column or porous H i geometry. Small Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha peak offsets or separations and high f esc Ly ​ α f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Ly\alpha} are empirically associated with direct LyC emitters, although with substantial scatter and a strong dependence on viewing angle and neutral-gas geometry ( Verhamme et al., 2015 ; Verhamme et al., 2017 ; Izotov et al., 2018 ; Gazagnes et al., 2020 ; Flury et al., 2022 ; Naidu et al., 2022 ) . High O32 increases the probability of LyC leakage but is not sufficient on its own ( Jaskot & Oey, 2013 ; Nakajima & Ouchi, 2014 ; Flury et al., 2022 ; Choustikov et al., 2024 ) . Recent empirical applications therefore combine ionization-sensitive line ratios with UV slope and compactness ( Steidel et al., 2018 ; Pahl et al., 2021 ; Chisholm et al., 2022 ; Mascia et al., 2023 ; Mascia et al., 2024 ; Saxena et al., 2024 ) . The Mg II doublet provides a complementary resonant-line probe of low-column escape paths, subject to radiative-transfer and geometric degeneracies ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Henry et al., 2018 ; Chisholm et al., 2020 ; Katz et al., 2022 ) . Taken together, these properties are consistent with ionizing escape channels in MARTA 3887 but do not yield a quantitative estimate of the LyC escape fraction. Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha photons can scatter around optically thick material, whereas LyC photons are absorbed, and both escape processes are anisotropic; moreover, LyC photons that escape before producing recombinations also reduce H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha and Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha together and are not counted by their ratio. We consequently regard MARTA 3887 as a multi-proxy, though indirect LyC-leaker candidate. Finally, the presence of the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component naturally motivates a search for a broad Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha counterpart. We find no reproducible detection of such a component in the MUSE data: adding a direct, symmetric Gaussian with the broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha kinematics to the 0.8 ′′ 0.8^{\prime\prime} -extracted spectrum gives F Ly ​ α , b < 3.4 × 10 − 17 F_{\rm Ly\alpha,b}<3.4\times 10^{-17} erg s -1 cm -2 (one-sided 95% confidence). The mild preference for a non-zero component in the full-depth cube is however not reproduced in either of the two independent observing subsets and is therefore not interpreted as a detection. For comparison, the observed broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux predicts F Ly ​ α , b ≃ ( 0.6 CLOSE F_{\rm Ly\alpha,b}\simeq(0.6 – OPEN 1.5 ) × 10 − 17 1.5)\times 10^{-17} erg s -1 cm -2 for intrinsic Ly α \alpha /H α \alpha ratios ranging from a representative observed quasar-BLR value ( ≃ 3.3 \simeq 3.3 ; Kriss 1984 ) to Case B ( ≃ 8.8 \simeq 8.8 ), respectively, and before accounting for the partial IGM transmission of the blue wing at z = 3.77 z=3.77 . The present data are thus not sensitive enough to identify an unattenuated counterpart. At the same time, we note that the galaxy-integrated properties inferred for MARTA 3887, including the low E ​ ( B − V ) neb E(B-V)_{\rm neb} and high f esc Ly ​ α f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Ly\alpha} , do not necessarily apply to the sightline towards the compact nucleus. A modest nuclear dust column, to which the present broad- H ​ β {\rm H}\beta limit is insensitive (Sect. 3.2 ), would attenuate Ly α \alpha by roughly three–four times more than H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha Ṁoreover, in the case of a static, fully covering T ≃ 10 4 T\simeq 10^{4} K H i screen, N HI ∼ 10 20 N_{\rm HI}\sim 10^{20} cm -2 gives an optical depth of order unity even at ≃ 600 \simeq 600 km s -1 from line center. Resonant scattering can therefore increase the path length and effective dust attenuation of a compact nuclear Ly α \alpha component ( Neufeld, 1990 ; Dijkstra, 2014 , e.g.) . The extended and asymmetric Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission seen in the MUSE data therefore most likely traces galaxy-scale radiative transfer and does not directly probe the sub-pc BLR. We therefore treat both the observed profile and the absence of a reproducible broad component as neutral with respect to the AGN interpretation discussed below.

sections.heading: 6.1 A broad-line AGN candidate
sections.text: The robust detection of a broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component (Sect. 3.1 ) provides the primary observational evidence for a low-mass accreting black hole in MARTA 3887. We adopt the BLR interpretation for the quantitative inferences below, while retaining such scenario as conditional because the present single-epoch data cannot exclude every transient or compact high-density alternative. The broad component is confined to the permitted H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission, is centered close to systemic, and is substantially wider than narrow and outflow-like components. No comparably broad forbidden-line counterpart is required by the data (Sect. 3.2 ), while any constraint on the broad H ​ β {\rm H}\beta remains weak ( S / N ≲ 2 \mathrm{S/N}\lesssim 2 ). No X-ray counterpart is present in the Chandra COSMOS-Legacy or XMM-COSMOS point-source catalogues ( Cappelluti et al., 2009 ; Civano et al., 2016 ; Marchesi et al., 2016 ) ; however, the more constraining Chandra soft-band depth corresponds to L 2 − 10 ​ keV ≲ ( 3.5 CLOSE L_{2-10\,\mathrm{keV}}\lesssim(3.5 – OPEN 5 ) × 10 43 5)\times 10^{43} erg s -1 . Adopting the luminosity-dependent 2 2 – 10 10 keV bolometric correction of Duras et al. (2020) , including its intrinsic scatter, predicts an X-ray flux more than an order of magnitude below the catalogue depth for the fiducial broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha -based L bol L_{\rm bol} . The non-detection therefore provides no meaningful constraint on the BLR interpretation, particularly because X-ray weakness is common among faint JWST broad-line AGN ( Ananna et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2024a ; Maiolino et al., 2025 ; Geris et al., 2026 ) . Under the BLR interpretation, we estimate the black-hole mass with a single-epoch virial relation. For consistency with recent literature compilations such as that analysing the JADES sample ( Juodžbalis et al., 2026 ) , we adopt the Reines & Volonteri (2015) broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha calibration, log ⁡ M BH M ⊙ = 6.60 + 0.47 ​ log ⁡ L H ​ α , b 10 42 ​ erg ​ s − 1 + 2.06 ​ log ⁡ FWHM H ​ α , b 10 3 ​ km ​ s − 1 , \begin{split}\log\frac{M_{\rm BH}}{M_{\odot}}={}&6.60+0.47\log\frac{L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}}{10^{42}\ {\rm erg\ s^{-1}}}\\ &+2.06\log\frac{{\rm FWHM}_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}}{10^{3}\ {\rm km\ s^{-1}}},\end{split} (1) which gives log ⁡ ( M BH / M ⊙ ) = 6.52 − 0.23 + 0.18 \log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23} from the statistical line uncertainties, while we retain a separate 0.30-dex systematic uncertainty term for the single-epoch calibration. The Greene & Ho (2005) prescription instead gives log ⁡ ( M BH / M ⊙ ) = 6.17 \log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=6.17 , and we use it to illustrate the calibration systematics. Alternatives to the black-hole scenario can be assessed directly against the properties of MARTA 3887. The non-core [O iii ]-emitting component has an intrinsic FWHM = 299 {\rm FWHM}=299 km s -1 , substantially narrower than broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha . Assigning its kinematics simultaneously to H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha and both [N ii ] lines does not reproduce the observed H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha +[N ii ] base: this intermediate-complex model is disfavoured relative to broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha by Δ ​ BIC = 41.8 \Delta{\rm BIC}=41.8 (Appendix B ). Together with the absence of a forbidden-line component of comparable width and the spatial-profile tests, this result rules out aperture smearing and disfavours an ordinary low- or moderate-density galaxy-scale outflow. A separate compact phase with densities approaching or exceeding the [O iii ] λ ​ 5008 \lambda 5008 critical density could suppress its forbidden emission and cannot be excluded by the present data. A luminous interacting core-collapse SN remains the principal transient alternative. The measured L H ​ α , b = 2.35 × 10 41 L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=2.35\times 10^{41} erg s -1 and FWHM ≃ 1270 {\rm FWHM}\simeq 1270 km s -1 are attainable by Type IIn-like events. For the measured SFR H ​ α = 9.3 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 {\rm SFR}_{\rm H\alpha}=9.3\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} , the time-averaged scaling adopted in recent assessments of JWST broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha sources predicts L H ​ α , b SN ≃ 5.6 × 10 40 L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}^{\rm SN}\simeq 5.6\times 10^{40} erg s -1 , approximately 4.2 times below the observed luminosity ( Maiolino et al., 2025 ; Geris et al., 2026 ) . We stress that this comparison concerns the mean contribution of the underlying SN population and is not an upper limit on a single event: an individual luminous interacting SN could in fact reach the observed luminosity, provided it is caught during the comparatively brief phase in which broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha is strong ( Kiewe et al., 2012 ; Taddia et al., 2013 ; Smith, 2017 ) . Nonetheless, the nearly systemic and approximately symmetric profile, without an obvious P-Cygni feature nor the large late-time blueshift often produced by dust in SN ejecta, still favours the BLR interpretation ( Gall et al., 2014 ) .
