The factor of ≈ 5 \approx 5 between the two λ Edd \lambda_{\rm Edd} estimates arises from combining the alternative bolometric conversion —raising L bol L_{\rm bol} by 0.36 dex— with the alternative virial relation which lowers M BH M_{\rm BH} by 0.35 dex; changing either calibration alone gives λ Edd ≃ 0.17 \lambda_{\rm Edd}\simeq 0.17 . The Harikane et al. (2023) -like conversion implies an AGN continuum of 39.7 nJy at observed 2.432 ​ μ 2.432\,\mu m, well above the slope-dependent 95% limits of 8.3–12.2 nJy from the simultaneous host+AGN fits (Sect. 4 ). Both bolometric chains, like the single-epoch virial relations, are calibrated primarily on lower-redshift Type-1 AGN and are extrapolated here to a low-mass z = 3.77 z=3.77 source. We also note that in both chains the quantities entering λ Edd \lambda_{\rm Edd} inherit the broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha luminosity and are therefore highly covariant. We therefore leave the full λ Edd ≃ 0.07 \lambda_{\rm Edd}\simeq 0.07 –0.38 bracket as a conservative systematic uncertainty, and show the results from alternative calibration chains as connected open symbols in Fig. 11 . From the fiducial host stellar mass we infer M BH / M ⋆ = 2.3 % M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}=2.3\% . The adoption of an unregularized-SFH would raise this to ≃ 6.6 % \simeq 6.6\% , whereas the simultaneous host+AGN fits change the stellar mass by less than 0.05 dex. This is 0.36 dex above the M BH / M ⋆ = 1 % M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}=1\% locus of the JADES sample ( Juodžbalis et al., 2026 ) , and lies well above the local broad-line AGN relation of Reines & Volonteri (2015) , although that relation is only weakly anchored at the stellar mass of MARTA 3887. The Kormendy & Ho (2013) relation is shown only for visual reference, since it is calibrated against classical-bulge mass and is not directly applicable to the total stellar mass of a clumpy, star-forming galaxy. The alternative virial calibration yields M BH / M ⋆ ≃ 1.0 % M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}\simeq 1.0\% , close to the JADES mean locus, without bringing the source onto the local broad-line AGN relation. In Fig. 11 we separate statistical errors from the 0.30-dex virial and bolometric systematics; the host-mass outer uncertainty is asymmetric and incorporates the explicitly explored SFH and old-population tests (see also Appendix D.3 ). We also note that our comparison adopts the stellar mass of the integrated system, whereas the morphology of MARTA 3887 is dominated by at least two bright components that are both captured by the NIRSpec slit (Fig. 1 and Sect. 4.1 ). The NIRSpec spectra do not localize the broad component to either of the two clumps; should it be associated with only one of them, the physically relevant host mass would be smaller and the local M BH / M ⋆ M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star} ratio correspondingly higher. Taken at face value, the offset measured for MARTA 3887 implies that its black hole assembled rapidly relative to the presently observed stellar host, compatible with a phase in which black-hole growth leads stellar assembly. A massive seed—including a direct-collapse black hole (DCBH)—merger-triggered or otherwise bursty super-Eddington growth, and subsequent feedback-regulated evolution can all produce such a state ( Inayoshi et al., 2020 ; Pacucci & Loeb, 2024 ; Trinca et al., 2026 , e.g.) . The stacked analysis of Geris et al. (2026) provides relevant population context, suggesting the presence of an average population at 3 < z < 7 3<z<7 with log ⁡ ( M BH / M ⊙ ) ≃ 6.2 \log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})\simeq 6.2 –6.6 and λ Edd ≃ 0.02 \lambda_{\rm Edd}\simeq 0.02 –0.1 sharing the same low-mass, moderately accreting regime probed by our fiducial MARTA 3887 estimates. At 3 < z < 5 3<z<5 , their inferred active black-hole mass function at a few times 10 6 ​ M ⊙ 10^{6}\,M_{\odot} is ( 3.1 CLOSE (3.1 – OPEN 8.7 ) × 10 − 3 ​ Mpc − 3 ​ dex − 1 8.7)\times 10^{-3}\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}\,{\rm dex}^{-1} . The inferred black-hole mass function is well reproduced by the active subset of the cat framework ( Trinca et al., 2022 ) in which black holes grow through short, episodic super-Eddington phases ( Trinca et al., 2026 ; Geris et al., 2026 ) . In the specific model comparison presented by Geris et al. (2026) , heavy-seed realizations also provide a closer match than models restricted to light seeds and Eddington-limited growth. More generally, however, seeding and accretion remain strongly degenerate: efficient growth can allow both light and heavy seeds to populate the observed region and progressively erase their initial mass differences ( Habouzit et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Koudmani et al., 2026 ; Dayal, 2026 ) . By z ≃ 3.8 z\simeq 3.8 , subsequent accretion may have erased much of the information about the initial conditions, so the position of MARTA 3887 alone cannot identify its black-hole seed (we further explore some of the possibilities in Sect. 6.3 ). The same population comparison cautions against interpreting individual offsets as direct evidence for evolution of the normalization of the entire M BH M_{\rm BH} – M ⋆ M_{\star} relation. Broad-line flux and line-width thresholds preferentially select massive, actively accreting black holes at fixed host mass, while measurement scatter moves objects into the detectable upper envelope ( Li et al., 2025 ) . Stacking analyses recover lower-mass and less actively accreting black holes whose mean locations lie closer to the local relation than those of individual detections. Nevertheless, the stacked measurements remain, on average, above the local relation and do not establish whether a corresponding population exists below it. This is consistent with individually detected AGN preferentially sampling the upper- M BH M_{\rm BH} tail at fixed host mass. Furthermore, host detectability introduces an additional selection effect, and stellar masses depend on properly separating nuclear from stellar light, while the resolved NIRCam morphology and < 10.3 % <10.3\% conditional limit on the emergent AGN continuum at 5100 Å reduce this ambiguity for MARTA 3887.

sections.heading: 6.3 Co-evolution of black-hole and galaxy host
sections.text: Figure 12 compares the posterior host SFH and cumulative formed mass with illustrative black-hole growth tracks 7 7 7 These tracks are not inferred black-hole growth histories on the same lookback-time axis. The stellar-mass assembly times t 10 t_{10} and t 50 t_{50} do not constrain the formation time of the seed or the onset of accretion; we use them only to construct limiting scenarios in which black-hole growth begins as late as the dominant observed episode of stellar assembly. To build the latter, we assume a single seed branch with no black-hole mergers after t seed t_{\rm seed} , M BH ​ ( t ) = M seed ​ exp ⁡ [ ⟨ λ Edd ⟩ ​ ( t − t seed ) t Sal ] , M_{\rm BH}(t)=M_{\rm seed}\exp\left[\frac{\langle\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}\rangle(t-t_{\rm seed})}{t_{\rm Sal}}\right], (2) with constant mean Eddington ratio ⟨ λ Edd ⟩ \langle\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}\rangle , radiative efficiency ϵ = 0.1 \epsilon=0.1 , and Salpeter time t Sal = 0.05 t_{\rm Sal}=0.05 Gyr ( Salpeter, 1964 ) . Each track is normalized to reach the fiducial log ⁡ ( M BH / M ⊙ ) = 6.52 \log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=6.52 at the observed epoch. Seeds of 10 2 10^{2} , 10 4 10^{4} , and 10 5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{5}\,M_{\odot} placed at an illustrative cosmic age of 0.1 Gyr (corresponding to z ∼ 30 \sim 30 , i.e. the left edge of Fig. 12 ) require ⟨ λ Edd ⟩ ≃ 0.34 \langle\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}\rangle\simeq 0.34 , 0.19, and 0.11, respectively. Imposing the median t 10 = 92 t_{10}=92 Myr as the start of accretion would instead require ⟨ λ Edd ⟩ ≃ 5.7 \langle\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}\rangle\simeq 5.7 for a 10 2 ​ M ⊙ 10^{2}\,M_{\odot} seed, rising to ≃ 29 \simeq 29 if growth began at t 50 = 18 t_{50}=18 Myr. Repeating the calculation with the lower Greene & Ho (2005) mass changes the early-seed values to 0.31, 0.16, and 0.087. We stress that the inferred lifetime-mean Eddington ratios depend on the adopted final mass but not on the estimate of the instantaneous λ Edd \lambda_{\rm Edd} , as they assume a constant radiative efficiency of ϵ = 0.1 \epsilon=0.1 and parameterize the time-averaged mass growth. As such, they should not be interpreted as luminosities known to have been reached at any particular epoch, but in our no-merger scenario they only describe the accretion required along one progenitor branch; mergers with other seed-bearing progenitors would reduce that requirement. Relatedly, the resolved clumpy morphology of MARTA 3887 is compatible with, though does not firmly establish, assembly through a galaxy merger. In particular, the NIRSpec spectrum contains no spectroscopic evidence for two BLRs or for a dual active nucleus. Any black-hole merger relevant to the mass assembly of MARTA 3887 would therefore have occurred earlier in its merger tree and cannot be reconstructed from the current morphology or integrated spectra. Spatially resolved spectroscopy is required to distinguish genuine dual AGN from non-AGN clumps, chance alignments, or lensing in multiple systems ( Perna et al., 2023 ; Scialpi et al., 2024 ; Übler et al., 2024 ) . The three adopted seed masses are intended to bracket the main families of proposed formation pathways. The 10 2 ​ M ⊙ 10^{2}\,M_{\odot} track is representative of light seeds left by massive Pop III stars ( Madau & Rees, 2001 ) ; the 10 4 ​ M ⊙ 10^{4}\,M_{\odot} track represents intermediate-mass seeds assembled through runaway stellar collisions, repeated mergers, and gas accretion in dense primordial or nuclear star clusters ( Portegies Zwart et al., 2004 ; Devecchi & Volonteri, 2009 ; Boekholt et al., 2018 ) ; and the 10 5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{5}\,M_{\odot} track corresponds to the characteristic mass scale of heavy seeds formed through the collapse of supermassive stars in atomic-cooling haloes ( Bromm & Loeb, 2003 ; Begelman et al., 2006 ; Lodato & Natarajan, 2006 ; Inayoshi et al., 2020 ) . In the classical DCBH picture, rapid inflow in an atomic-cooling halo forms a ∼ 10 4 \sim 10^{4} – 10 6 ​ M ⊙ 10^{6}\,M_{\odot} seed before ordinary star formation fragments the gas; this generally requires pristine or only very weakly enriched gas, together with conditions that suppress H 2 cooling ( Omukai et al., 2008 ; Inayoshi et al., 2020 ) . In this sense, the low metallicity measured in MARTA 3887, 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) = 7.68 12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68 ( ≃ 0.10 ​ Z ⊙ \simeq 0.10\penalty\ Z_{\odot} ), is qualitatively consistent with a chemically young host and, while being already far above the metallicities normally required for the classical DCBH channel, it refers to the ionized gas observed at z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 , long after any plausible seed-formation epoch. The seed could moreover have formed in a different, initially pristine branch of the merger tree before entering the presently observed, mildly enriched system. More in general, the metallicity of the host galaxy may provide an additional constraint even when efficient accretion has erased much of the seed-mass imprint from the M BH M_{\rm BH} – M ⋆ M_{\star} plane. In the aesopica simulations, however, a clear separation emerges only in the more extreme regime M BH / M ⋆ > 0.1 M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}>0.1 and Z / Z ⊙ < 0.01 Z/Z_{\odot}<0.01 , which is populated exclusively by heavy-seed models at z = 7 z=7 ( Koudmani et al., 2026 ) . MARTA 3887, with M BH / M ⋆ ≃ 0.023 M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}\simeq 0.023 and Z / Z ⊙ ≃ 0.10 Z/Z_{\odot}\simeq 0.10 , lies outside this regime, where the predicted seed populations overlap substantially. Its metallicity therefore strengthens the characterization of the host as chemically young, but does not currently favour a light- or heavy-seed origin. The comparison is also not strictly like-for-like, because our metallicity is an emission-weighted H ii -region oxygen abundance measurement, whereas the simulations do not resolve the multiphase metallicity structure sampled by the nebular lines. The constant- ⟨ λ Edd ⟩ \langle\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}\rangle curves further compress a potentially intermittent accretion history into one time-averaged parameter. Models developed for the JWST broad-line population commonly predict feedback-regulated cycles in which short super-Eddington episodes can provide a substantial fraction of the integrated mass growth. For instance, the semi-analytic framework of Trinca et al. (2026) produces repeated 0.5–3 Myr bursts with duty cycles of 1–4%, while the cosmological aesopica simulations find model-dependent bursts lasting approximately 10 Myr and super-Eddington fractions of only about 0.2–2% at z = 4 z=4 ( Koudmani et al., 2026 ) . The difference in timescale reflects the adopted accretion and feedback prescriptions, but both results illustrate that a black hole observed at the fiducial instantaneous λ Edd = 0.07 \lambda_{\rm Edd}=0.07 may have experienced much more rapid earlier episodes. Efficient accretion can also erase much of the seed-mass imprint by z ∼ 4 z\sim 4 ( Koudmani et al., 2026 ) , further limiting what the current mass and host SFH alone can reveal about the initial seeding. Taken together, the proposed analysis does not allow us to date the formation of the black-hole seed precisely, nor to establish whether it pre-dated the galaxy. The exercise nevertheless excludes a restricted but physically informative scenario: under the adopted no-merger, ϵ = 0.1 \epsilon=0.1 assumptions, a light seed whose growth began only during the dominant recent episode of stellar assembly could not reach the observed mass through sustained sub-Eddington accretion. At least one of the following is therefore required: an earlier onset of black-hole growth, a more massive seed, intermittent episodes of rapid accretion, or growth through black-hole mergers. The comparison thus identifies a mismatch between the rapid recent assembly of the surviving stellar host and the time required to build the inferred black-hole mass, while remaining unable to determine whether black-hole growth preceded, accompanied, or followed the full assembly history of the galaxy. sections.heading: 6.4 Low-column-density gas and the possible link to LyC leakage
sections.text: The provisional Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha escape fraction, the small Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha velocity offset, the Mg II ratio near its optically thin value, the high O32 value, and low metallicity consistently point toward a low effective H I column or porous, anisotropic gas geometry. As already noted in Sect. 5 , MUSE cannot measure the LyC directly: at z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 the Lyman limit is observed at 4349 Å, below its blue cutoff, and MARTA 3887 should therefore be considered as an indirect LyC-leaker candidate. The existing HST imaging nevertheless provides some direct observational constraints (see Figure D1 ). In fact, WFC3/F336W probes the SED below the redshifted Lyman limit (its pivot wavelength corresponds to ≃ 703 \simeq 703 Å in the rest frame) and gives a 3 ​ σ 3\sigma upper limit of f ν < 0.46 f_{\nu}<0.46 nJy ( m AB > 32.24 m_{\rm AB}>32.24 ), delivering no direct LyC detection; ACS/F435W is detected at 3.4 ​ σ 3.4\sigma , but the filter straddles 4349 Å and includes transmission redward of the Lyman edge. Converting the F336W limit into an absolute f esc LyC f_{\rm esc}^{\rm LyC} would require the intrinsic stellar-plus-AGN ionizing spectrum and marginalization over the strongly stochastic IGM+CGM transmission ( Inoue et al., 2014 ; Bassett et al., 2021 ; Steidel et al., 2018 ; Pahl et al., 2021 ) ; this is especially important because F336W probes the far LyC near 700 Å, where the line-of-sight transmission at this redshift can be very small. Direct LyC surveys at z ≃ 3 z\simeq 3 consequently infer escape fractions statistically over ensembles or explicitly forward-model sightline transmission rather than treating a single non-detection as an intrinsic constraint ( Steidel et al., 2018 ; Pahl et al., 2021 ) . The photometry therefore constrains the product of internal escape and IGM transmission and cannot isolate f esc LyC f_{\rm esc}^{\rm LyC} ; the F336W non-detection neither confirms nor rules out the low-column channels suggested by the emission line diagnostics. The presence of an accreting black hole in MARTA 3887 does not imply that escaping ionizing photons are AGN-powered; the full budget is Q ⁡ ( H ) = Q ​ ( H ) ⋆ + Q ​ ( H ) AGN Q({\rm H})=Q({\rm H})_{\star}+Q({\rm H})_{\rm AGN} , with potentially distinct stellar and AGN escape fractions. The narrow, extended Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission probes transfer through host/NLR-scale gas and cannot identify the ionizing source. The available data cannot determine whether any low-covering-factor geometry is produced by stellar feedback, AGN activity, or the intrinsic structure of the multi-clump system; an AGN contribution is possible but not required. At z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 , the stochastic IGM transmission at the rest-frame wavelengths sampled by F336W and the uncertain AGN EUV contribution make any absolute f esc LyC f_{\rm esc}^{\rm LyC} estimate weak and strongly model-dependent. We therefore do not infer an intrinsic LyC escape fraction from the available HST imaging.

sections.heading: 7 Summary and conclusions
sections.text: We have presented a multi-wavelength study of MARTA 3887, a compact, clumpy galaxy at z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 possibly hosting a low-mass accreting black hole, combining deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and archival VLT/MUSE data. Our analysis was designed to establish the origin of its broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission, characterize the stellar and ionized gas properties of the galaxy, and place the inferred black hole properties in the context of the low-mass AGN population now emerging from JWST surveys. Our principal results and conclusions are summarized below. • JWST/NIRSpec detects broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission with L H ​ α , b = 2.35 × 10 41 L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=2.35\times 10^{41} erg s -1 and FWHM = 1270 − 250 + 260 {\rm FWHM}=1270^{+260}_{-250} km s -1 (Sect. 3.1 , Fig. 2 ). Such a component is robust against the adopted continuum, line-spread function, and narrow-line model, is spatially coincident with the narrow-line emission, and has no comparably broad [O iii ] counterpart (Sect. 3.2 , Fig. 3 ; Appendix B , Fig. B1 ). These properties favour a broad-line region origin; an interacting supernova or a compact, high-density outflow are less likely, though they cannot be fully excluded with single-epoch data (Sect. 6.1 ). • The narrow-line spectrum is consistent with high-excitation, metal-poor gas. Assuming stellar-dominated photoionization, a joint inference of the physical conditions gives E ​ ( B − V ) neb = 0.054 ± 0.013 E(B-V)_{\rm neb}=0.054\pm 0.013 , T e ​ ( O ​ III ) = 18,140 − 710 + 770 T_{\rm e}({\rm O\,III})=18{,}140^{+770}_{-710} K, and 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) = 7.68 ± 0.04 12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm 0.04 (Sects. 3.3.1 and 3.3.4 , Fig. 5 ). The detection of [Ne iv ] points to an additional high-ionization phase, for which the doublet ratio limits the density to n e < 9.5 × 10 3 n_{\rm e}<9.5\times 10^{3} cm -3 (Sect. 3.3.2 , Fig. 6 ); together with the position of MARTA 3887 on diagnostic diagrams (Sect. 3.3.3 , Fig. 7 ), this is compatible with a modest contribution from the NLR of the AGN. Multi-cloud photoionization modeling reproduce the spectrum with an energetically consistent AGN component powering ≲ 10 % \lesssim 10\% of the narrow H β \beta flux; the model-based abundances ( 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) ≃ 7.8 12+\log({\rm O/H})\simeq 7.8 ) imply a systematic upward uncertainty of ≃ 0.15 \simeq 0.15 dex on the T e T_{\rm e} -based value, independent of the AGN contribution (Sect. 3.3.4 ; Appendix C , Fig. C1 ). • Morphologically, MARTA 3887 comprises at least three components, well resolved in the rest-frame UV imaging and separated by 0.8 0.8 – 1.2 1.2 proper kpc (Sect. 4.1 , Figs. 1 and 8 ; Appendix D.2 ). SED fitting to the integrated photometry gives log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) = 8.16 − 0.10 + 0.09 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10} and a rising recent SFH, with a 100-Myr-averaged SFR = 1.44 − 0.41 + 0.33 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 {\rm SFR}=1.44^{+0.33}_{-0.41}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} and SFR 0 − 10 ​ Myr = 5.42 − 0.52 + 0.77 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 {\rm SFR}_{0-10\,{\rm Myr}}=5.42^{+0.77}_{-0.52}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} (Sect. 4.2 , Fig. 9 ), the latter consistent with the aperture- and dust-corrected narrow-H α \alpha estimate of 9.3 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 9.3\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1} within the systematics (Sect. 4.3 ). • Under the broad-line region interpretation, the fiducial virial calibration gives log ⁡ ( M BH / M ⊙ ) = 6.52 − 0.23 + 0.18 \log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23} and λ Edd = 0.07 \lambda_{\rm Edd}=0.07 , with alternative calibration chains spanning λ Edd = 0.07 \lambda_{\rm Edd}=0.07 – 0.38 0.38 (Sects. 6.1 and 6.2 ). The resulting M BH / M ⋆ = 2.3 % M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}=2.3\% lies approximately 2 dex above the (extrapolated) local relation for broad-line AGN, placing MARTA 3887 at the edge of the low-mass end of current JWST samples (Sect. 6.2 , Fig. 11 ). In an illustrative no-merger scenario with constant radiative efficiency, a light seed whose growth began only with the dominant recent episode of stellar assembly could reach the inferred mass only through sustained super-Eddington accretion ( ⟨ λ Edd ⟩ ≃ 5.7 \langle\lambda_{\rm Edd}\rangle\simeq 5.7 ). Earlier onset of accretion, a more massive seed, intermittent rapid episodes, or black-hole mergers would relax this requirement, but the host SFH and present ISM properties cannot discriminate among these histories (Sect. 6.3 , Fig. 12 ). • MUSE resolves asymmetric Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission over a 6.5–6.9 proper-kpc major-axis FWHM, with L Ly ​ α = 1.39 × 10 43 L_{\rm Ly\alpha}=1.39\times 10^{43} erg s -1 , an intrinsic FWHM of 245 − 22 + 21 245^{+21}_{-22} km s -1 , and a peak offset of + 64 − 8 + 10 +64^{+10}_{-8} km s -1 (Sect. 5 , Fig. 10 ). The provisional f esc Ly ​ α ≃ 0.44 f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Ly\alpha}\simeq 0.44 , the small Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha velocity offset, the Mg II doublet ratio ( R MgII = 1.90 − 0.22 + 0.27 R_{\rm MgII}=1.90^{+0.27}_{-0.22} ; Sect. 3.3.5 ), and the high O32 consistently point to low-column-density or porous sightlines. Altogether, they make MARTA 3887 a strong, indirect LyC-leaker candidate, although the available data cannot measure the LyC escape fraction nor establish any direct causal link with the AGN (Sect. 6.4 ). In conclusion, MARTA 3887 extends the individually detected population of accreting black holes into the metal-poor, M ⋆ ≃ 10 8 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}\simeq 10^{8}\,M_{\odot} host regime, offering a view of black-hole growth outpacing stellar assembly in a young, low-mass galaxy beyond cosmic noon.

sections.heading: Appendix A Aperture corrections on the NIRSpec spectrum
sections.text: The reduced one-dimensional NIRSpec products include the standard point-source path-loss and slit-loss correction. MARTA 3887 is nevertheless resolved into several compact knots, so this calibration does not recover the flux that would be measured by the 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} -radius aperture used for the integrated SED fitting. We here define the aperture-correction factor as C ap ≡ F 0.5 ′′ / F NIRSpec , ps C_{\rm ap}\equiv F_{0.5^{\prime\prime}}/F_{\rm NIRSpec,ps} , where the denominator is the flux returned by the point-source-calibrated one-dimensional extraction. We use this imaging-based correction only when the comparison is explicitly referred to the same 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture and a nearby NIRCam band provides a plausible morphological proxy for the quantity of interest, as F300M does e.g. for narrow H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha . For each NIRCam band, we projected the full central shutter onto the native image using the WCS and every MSA configuration that enters the extracted spectrum (39 G140M and 12 G235M integration/nod footprints, equal-weighted). We measured the admitted fraction of the 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture light and divided the corresponding NIRSpec point-source throughput by it. The three nod positions are repeated across the exposures, but retaining every footprint ensures that the adopted geometry follows the actual data combination. At the observed wavelength of H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha , the direct F300M image proxy gives C ap = 1.76 − 0.09 + 0.06 C_{\rm ap}=1.76^{+0.06}_{-0.09} . We tested the imaging/spectroscopy PSF mismatch separately. We fitted the F300M morphology with three intrinsic Gaussian clumps convolved with the NIRCam STPSF, re-convolved the best-fit intrinsic model with the NIRSpec PSF at the wavelength of interest, and repeated the shutter calculation. This gives C ap = 1.67 − 0.03 + 0.05 C_{\rm ap}=1.67^{+0.05}_{-0.03} . An independent comparison of synthetic G235M photometry with the measured F300M 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} flux gives 1.83 − 0.21 + 0.27 1.83^{+0.27}_{-0.21} . We adopt the direct-image value for narrow H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha and use the envelope 1.64–2.10 as a conservative aperture-mapping systematic. We note that, although the inferred factor varies across the NIRCam bands, we do not interpolate it and rescale the complete spectrum. In fact, the imaging supplies a broad-band continuum proxy, while the true cross-dispersion morphology of every individual emission line remains unknown; a line-by-line application would therefore assume that all lines follow the nearby continuum morphology. Indeed, applying such broad-band factors to the Balmer series produces inconsistent decrements. The correction is consequently used only for the integrated narrow H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux in Sect. 4.3 , for which the target 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture and the F300M proxy are explicitly defined. For the Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha comparison in Sect. 5 , we use this aperture-corrected H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha flux under the additional assumption that the non-resonant recombination emission is compact (the larger r = 1.4 ′′ r=1.4^{\prime\prime} MUSE aperture preventing a strictly aperture-matched escape fraction calculation). All other narrow-line ratios, and associated diagnostics, retain the values inferred directly from fitting the pipeline-calibrated NIRSpec spectrum. Finally, the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component is treated as a point-like source and retains the native pipeline calibration, with no further correction applied.

sections.heading: Appendix B Broad H α \alpha robustness tests
sections.text: Because the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component is detected at modest contrast against a much brighter narrow line, we here test its width recovery against different choices in the local spectral model and the resolved morphology of the source. Starting from the fiducial fit described in Sect. 3.1 , we repeated the analysis while changing the fitted wavelength interval, the polynomial order of the continuum, the inclusion of the adjacent [S ii ] lines, and the constraints on the narrow component. Furthermore, we also replaced the fiducial scaled uniformly illuminated-slit LSF with the nominal uniform-slit and point-source prescriptions ( de Graaff et al. 2024 ) , and allowed a Gauss–Hermite rather than Gaussian broad profile. In all cases, we found that including a broad component is favoured by the data. For the cases in which the narrow-line kinematics is left free, the inferred broad flux lies within ( 1.53 CLOSE (1.53 – OPEN 1.77 ) × 10 − 18 1.77)\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 , the intrinsic FWHM within 1200–1480 km s -1 , and − 52 < Δ ​ BIC < − 41 -52<\Delta{\rm BIC}<-41 . The inferred broad component properties are therefore mostly insensitive to the continuum and LSF choices explored here. The [O iii ] fit independently identifies a non-core component with FWHM = 299 {\rm FWHM}=299 km s -1 and Δ ​ v = − 61 \Delta v=-61 km s -1 (Sect. 3.2 ). We test whether the apparent broad base could instead arise from the blending of intermediate-width H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha and [N ii ] emission by assigning these three lines the measured [O iii ] kinematics, while fixing the [N ii ] doublet ratio. The same component is also allowed for the [S ii ] doublet over the wider fitted window. This intermediate-complex model is disfavoured relative to the fiducial broad- H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha model by Δ ​ BIC = 41.8 \Delta{\rm BIC}=41.8 . Adding broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha to the intermediate-complex model improves its BIC by 28.2, whereas retaining the intermediate components in addition to broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha is not supported. In the combined fit, the broad component has F H ​ α , b = 1.56 × 10 − 18 F_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1.56\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 and FWHM = 1246 {\rm FWHM}=1246 km s -1 , consistent with the fiducial measurements. Thus, the detected [O iii ] wing cannot account for the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha base. Compact shocks or high-density outflows remain possible because their forbidden emission may be collisionally suppressed, but they are not favoured over the broad-line model by the present data. Next, we quantified the statistical recovery of the broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component with three complementary resampling experiments. First, 350 parametric bootstrap realizations generated from the fiducial broad-line model have a median F H ​ α , b = 1.76 × 10 − 18 F_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1.76\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 . We retain the reference-fit value, 1.69 × 10 − 18 1.69\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 , as the fiducial centre and recenter the bootstrap percentile widths on it, giving the 1.69 − 0.19 + 0.26 × 10 − 18 1.69^{+0.26}_{-0.19}\times 10^{-18} interval quoted in Sect. 3.1 . The same bootstrap gives FWHM H ​ α , b = 1270 − 250 + 260 {\rm FWHM}_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1270^{+260}_{-250} km s -1 . Second, we injected components with FWHM of 800, 1400, and 2000 km s -1 over a range of line fluxes and refitted each realization with both the narrow-only and broad-line models. At 1.5 × 10 − 18 1.5\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 , i.e. close to the actual measured flux, 80–100% of the trials meet the conservative Δ ​ BIC < − 10 \Delta{\rm BIC}<-10 criterion; the recovery fraction reaches unity for every tested width by 2.0 × 10 − 18 2.0\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 (Fig. B1 (a)). The median recovered fluxes and widths track the injected values without evidence for a preferential positive-flux bias. Finally, none of 250 spectra simulated from the best-fitting narrow-only model produces a BIC improvement as large as the observed Δ ​ BIC = − 46.8 \Delta{\rm BIC}=-46.8 ; the 1st–99th percentile interval of the null distribution is 6.8 < Δ ​ BIC < 14.5 6.8<\Delta{\rm BIC}<14.5 . Finally, the two-dimensional G235M spectrum provides a separate test of morphological broadening. Because MARTA 3887 is resolved within the shutter, the narrow-line trace is slightly tilted along the dispersion direction. Figure B1 (b) shows the core and symmetric wing intervals used to construct the continuum-subtracted profiles in Figure B1 (c). The wing emission is centred on the positive-nod signal: its centroid differs from that of the narrow core by only 0.14 ± 0.11 0.14\pm 0.11 spatial pixels, and its fitted spatial width, σ = 1.17 ± 0.16 \sigma=1.17\pm 0.16 pixels, is consistent with the narrow-core value of 1.145 ± 0.009 1.145\pm 0.009 pixels. Thus the spectral wings are spatially associated with MARTA 3887 rather than with a displaced contaminant. Moreover, collapsing templates based on the resolved narrow trace or on the adjacent continuum does not reproduce the wavelength extent of the broad base, showing that the tilted narrow-line morphology alone cannot account for the flux excess in the wings as seen in the one-dimensional spectrum. In conclusion, the spectral decomposition, resampling experiments, and two-dimensional tests demonstrate that the measured broad component is not an artefact of the adopted continuum, LSF, noise realization, or resolved narrow-line trace, corroborating the scenario at the base of the interpretation presented in Sect. 6.1 . sections.heading: Appendix C HOMERUN photoionization decomposition
sections.text: homerun represents an observed emission-line spectrum as a non-negative weighted linear combination of constant-density, single-cloud Cloudy photoionization models ( Marconi et al. 2024 ; Ferland et al. 2017 ) . At a given chemical composition and incident continuum, the library spans electron density and ionization parameter; the cloud weights are determined by minimizing the homerun loss function. This construction allows different transitions to arise predominantly from different regions of the ( n e , U ) (n_{\rm e},U) grid rather than imposing a single characteristic density and ionization parameter on the integrated spectrum. The minimum-loss solution is identified separately for each metallicity and ionizing continuum, as described in detail by Marconi et al. (2024) and Moreschini et al. (2026) (see also Castellano et al. (2026) for another application to a high-z galaxy). We fitted the narrow-line measurements and limits listed in Table F . The stellar-only family contains clouds illuminated by the adopted stellar continuum, while the composite family combines independent stellar- and AGN-ionized cloud ensembles. To test whether the hard detected lines can be reproduced without an AGN, the stellar grid is extended to log ⁡ U = + 0.5 \log U=+0.5 , beyond the log ⁡ U ≤ − 1 \log U\leq-1 range normally adopted for the standard H ii -region grid. For the composite family we impose the fiducial f AGN ​ ( H ​ β ) ≤ 10 % f_{\rm AGN}({\rm H}\beta)\leq 10\% prior described in Sect. 3.3.4 . We explored separate attenuation configurations for the two components and recovered only small fitted extinctions. The comparison in the main text is based on the objective-function minima within each model family; these values provide a relative model ranking and are not interpreted as formal χ 2 \chi^{2} probabilities. Figure C1 summarizes the metallicity search and the structure of the best-fitting composite solution. The stellar-only and stellar+AGN families reach their minimum loss at 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) = 7.79 12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.79 and 7.81, respectively, compared with the fiducial direct-method value of 7.68 ± 0.04 7.68\pm 0.04 . The shallow, nearly coincident minima show directly that adding the adopted AGN continuum has little effect on the model-based abundance. The non-zero cloud weights span more than one density and ionization parameter in both components: the stellar ensemble is weighted mainly towards log ⁡ U ≃ − 2 \log U\simeq-2 , whereas the AGN ensemble includes both low-density, high-ionization gas and denser clouds with lower U U . These weights describe an unresolved emission-line mixture and should not be interpreted as distinct spatial zones. The lower panel of Fig. C1 shows how the composite solution partitions the predicted flux of each independent line constraint between the stellar and AGN components. The stellar component supplies 91% of H β \beta , 88% of H α \alpha , 87% of [O iii ] λ ​ 4363 \lambda 4363 , and 92% of [O iii ] λ ​ 5008 \lambda 5008 ; it also contributes more than 95% of both [O ii ] and Mg ii . By contrast, the detected [Ne iv ] emission is almost entirely assigned to AGN-ionized gas. The predicted He ii , [Ne v ], and [O i ] fluxes are likewise AGN dominated, but these transitions enter only as upper limits and therefore do not constitute additional detections of an AGN component. The [S ii ] doublet receives comparable contributions from the two components and is also the least accurately reproduced detected complex. The oxygen lines that set T e ​ ( O ​ iii ) T_{\rm e}({\rm O\,\textsc{iii}}) and dominate the abundance estimate therefore remain primarily associated with the stellar component. This explains why the inferred O/H changes by only 0.02 dex between the stellar-only and composite solutions. The detailed fractions remain conditional on the adopted model grids and on the H β \beta prior; they should not be interpreted as an observational separation of spatially distinct emitting regions. sections.heading: D.1 Image cutouts and integrated photometry
sections.text: Figure D1 presents all of the imaging data considered for MARTA 3887 on the same 1.6 ′′ 1.6^{\prime\prime} field. The HST panels in the first two rows establish the Lyman-break constraints discussed in Sect. 6.4 ; in particular, F336W is a non-detection, whereas F435W contains flux from both sides of the redshifted Lyman limit. The NIRCam panels from F090W to F460M show that the two principal knots and the fainter southern component are contained within the 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture used for the integrated photometry. F300M is displayed for completeness but excluded from the SED because it contains broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha , while the black F335M panel records missing coverage. The six MIRI panels in the bottom row contain no significant source at the target position and enter the fit only as upper limits. We measured the integrated fluxes in a common 0.5 ′′ 0.5^{\prime\prime} aperture, which includes all internal knots while avoiding the nearest external neighbour, and estimated the local background in a clipped 0.70 ′′ < r < 1.05 ′′ 0.70^{\prime\prime}<r<1.05^{\prime\prime} annulus. Before measurement, the NIRCam images were matched to the F460M PSF so that the aperture samples a consistent light fraction across filters; filter-dependent STPSF encircled-energy corrections were then applied. HST images were retained at their native resolution but measured with the same sky aperture. The MIRI images were likewise kept at their native PSFs, and their signed aperture measurements were converted into conservative total-flux limits using the appropriate encircled energies. The BAGPIPES likelihood treats detected HST and NIRCam bands as Gaussian measurements. For each MIRI band, it instead uses the Gaussian cumulative probability below the quoted 3 ​ σ 3\sigma limit ( Sawicki 2012 ) . This censored treatment preserves the information that bright rest-frame near-IR templates are disfavoured without assigning a positive flux to a non-detection, as shown in the ‘hidden-old-population test’ below. sections.heading: D.2 Multi-component morphology
sections.text: We fitted the native F090W, F115W, F150W, and F200W images with PSF-convolved Gaussian components. F200W defines the relative positions and intrinsic shapes, after which each filter has independent non-negative component amplitudes and a local sky plane. Each row of Figure D2 follows the five-panel decomposition used for the F150W fit in the main text: data, two-component model and residuals, and three-component model and residuals. Residuals are expressed in units of the pixel uncertainty. The third component is only marginal in F090W but is consistently recovered from F115W through F200W; over these three bands it contributes approximately 13–17% of the total light and removes the coherent southern residual left by the two-component model. To test for colour gradients across the system, we also fitted the fluxes of the three components in the remaining NIRCam images, while keeping their F200W positions and intrinsic shapes fixed and adopting the appropriate STPSF for each band. In the blue bands the clumps remain sufficiently well separated that their fitted fluxes are only weakly correlated ( | ρ | ≲ 0.25 |\rho|\lesssim 0.25 ). At 3.5–4.6 μ \mu m, the broader PSF blends them more strongly: flux can be exchanged between neighbouring components with little change in the total model, and the largest pairwise correlations increase to | ρ | = 0.24 |\rho|=0.24 – 0.45 0.45 . These correlations describe only the statistical degeneracy within the adopted model. They do not include systematic uncertainties from assuming that the intrinsic F200W morphology is unchanged at all wavelengths, from using a detector-centre STPSF rather than the effective position- and exposure-weighted PSF of the mosaic, or from genuine wavelength-dependent structures. Accordingly, we retain only the qualitative indication that the south-western component is redder than the north-eastern one, and we do not adopt the inferred fluxes to perform independent SED fitting at the clump level; all physical properties of the host remain inferred from the integrated photometry. Figure D2: PSF-convolved morphology fit in the native F090W, F115W, F150W, and F200W images. From left to right, each row shows the data, the two-component model and its residuals, and the three-component model and its residuals, normalized by the pixel uncertainty. The final panels report the BIC difference between the three- and two-component fits and the fitted light fraction of component C. The southern component is strongly preferred in F115W–F200W, where it removes the coherent residual below the two brighter knots.

sections.heading: D.3 Sensitivity to SFH priors and ‘maximally-old’ stress tests
sections.text: As a weakly regularized alternative to the fiducial continuity SFH model presented in Sect. 4.2 , we retain the same six time bins and parameter bounds but replace the Student- t t continuity terms with independent flat priors on the logarithmic adjacent-bin SFR ratios. This fit converges on a strongly rising, ≲ 5 \lesssim 5 Myr solution with log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) = 7.70 − 0.02 + 0.08 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})=7.70^{+0.08}_{-0.02} , 0.46 dex below the fiducial mass. Its best photometric likelihood is poorer than that of the scale-0.3 continuity fit by Δ ​ χ 2 = 7.5 \Delta\chi^{2}=7.5 . The experiment demonstrates the residual sensitivity of the host mass to the SFH prior; we retain the regularized solution as fiducial while including the full downward excursion in the asymmetric host-model systematic. Furthermore, the fiducial non-parametric SFH identifies the host galaxy growth as dominated by a recent star-formation episode, but cannot exclude the presence of a faint, high-mass-to-light-ratio population. We therefore constructed a ‘maximally old’ two-component model consisting of a 5–100 Myr burst, required to reproduce the young light, and an independent exponentially declining component whose onset is restricted to ages older than 200 Myr. This stress test attempts to quantify hidden mass and is not treated as an alternative preferred SFH. Figure D3 (a) shows the posterior formed mass of the old component. It peaks at a negligible contribution, with a median of 5.7 × 10 5 ​ M ⊙ 5.7\times 10^{5}\,M_{\odot} , but has a long prior-sensitive tail reaching 8.9 × 10 6 ​ M ⊙ 8.9\times 10^{6}\,M_{\odot} and 4.6 × 10 7 ​ M ⊙ 4.6\times 10^{7}\,M_{\odot} at the 84th and 95th percentiles. Figure D3 (b) expresses the same result as a fraction of the combined old-plus-young formed mass and gives f old < 0.22 f_{\rm old}<0.22 at 95% posterior probability. Repeating the experiment without the F1000W–F2100W limits relaxes the corresponding bounds to M old , formed < 2.0 × 10 8 ​ M ⊙ M_{\rm old,formed}<2.0\times 10^{8}\,M_{\odot} and f old < 0.62 f_{\rm old}<0.62 . The ensemble of MIRI non-detections therefore limits, but does not exclude, an older population. Figure D3: Posterior for the maximally-old test including all MIRI upper limits. Panel (a) shows the formed mass of the independent old component; panel (b) shows its fraction of the combined old-plus-young formed mass on a logarithmic axis. Solid black, dashed red, and dotted red lines mark the median, 84th percentile, and 95th percentile, respectively.

sections.heading: E.1 Astrometric registration and noise rescaling
sections.text: The archive MUSE world-coordinate system is displaced from the HST/JWST reference frame. We measured a rigid translation from three bright, isolated reference sources detected in both the MUSE white-light image and HST/F814W. The mean correction is ( Δ ​ α ​ cos ⁡ δ , Δ ​ δ ) HST − MUSE = ( − 0.348 ′′ , − 1.892 ′′ ) (\Delta\alpha\cos\delta,\Delta\delta)_{\rm HST-MUSE}=(-0.348^{\prime\prime},-1.892^{\prime\prime}) , with an rms scatter of approximately 0.03 ′′ 0.03^{\prime\prime} among the three matches. No additional rotation or scale term is required by this small reference set. Figure E1 shows the three reference matches and the effect of the correction. When the HST positions are projected using the archive MUSE WCS, they are displaced from the corresponding white-light sources by the common 1.92 ′′ 1.92^{\prime\prime} offset (red pluses in Fig. E1 a). The rigid translation moves them to the blue crosses, which coincide with the MUSE sources. The same correction moves the Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha narrow-band contours from the dashed red to the solid blue position in Fig. E1 (b). The registered Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha peak lies only 0.037 ′′ 0.037^{\prime\prime} from the NIRCam position, comparable to the registration rms. This corrected frame is used for the apertures, centroid, and spatial measurements reported in Sect. 5 . To account approximately for resampling covariance and residual sky structure not captured by the formal variance cube, we measure the wavelength-dependent scatter among 16 blank apertures around the source and rescale the spectral uncertainties accordingly. The same procedure is applied to the two constituent MUSE stacks (good and bad seeing). As an additional spatial check, the stack with better seeing gives a deconvolved major-axis FWHM of 0.89 ′′ 0.89^{\prime\prime} ( 6.5 6.5 proper kpc), consistent with the 0.95 ′′ 0.95^{\prime\prime} ( 6.9 6.9 proper kpc) measurement from the full-depth cube; the minor-axis size is less robust. Fermi 5, I-50125 Florence, Italy European Southern Observatory, Karl-Schwarzschild-Strasse 2, D-85748 Garching bei München, Germany Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge, 19 JJ Thomson Avenue, Cambridge CB3 0HE, UK Kavli Institute for Cosmology, University of Cambridge, Madingley Road, Cambridge CB3 0HA, UK Dipartimento di Fisica e Astronomia “Augusto Righi”, Alma Mater Studiorum – Università di Bologna, Via Piero Gobetti 93/2, I-40129 Bologna, Italy MIT Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 77 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Scuola Normale Superiore, Piazza dei Cavalieri 7, I-56126 Pisa, Italy ABSTRACT JWST has extended the search for accreting black holes into the high-redshift, low-mass regime, delivering unprecedented constraints on their formation path and seeding mechanisms. Here we report the discovery of a low-mass black hole candidate in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 . Combining deep JWST/NIRSpec MSA spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and archival VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy, we characterize the black hole, stellar host, and ionized gas properties of this system over the rest-frame UV-to-optical range. We identify a broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component with L H ​ α , b = 2.35 × 10 41 L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=2.35\times 10^{41} erg s -1 and FWHM = 1270 − 250 + 260 {\rm FWHM}=1270^{+260}_{-250} km s -1 , with no [O iii ] counterpart of comparable width. Under a broad-line-region interpretation, virial calibrations give log ⁡ ( M BH / M ⊙ ) = 6.52 − 0.23 + 0.18 \log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23} and λ Edd = L bol / L Edd = 0.07 \lambda_{\rm Edd}=L_{\rm bol}/L_{\rm Edd}=0.07 , or up to 0.38 0.38 for alternative calibrations. The host is resolved into three compact clumps, with integrated SED fitting yielding log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) = 8.16 − 0.10 + 0.09 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10} . The narrow-line spectrum is consistent with highly ionized, metal-poor gas, with 12 + log ⁡ ( O / H ) = 7.68 ± 0.04 12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm 0.04 ( ≃ 0.10 ​ Z ⊙ \simeq 0.10\,Z_{\odot} ). The inferred M BH / M ⋆ = 2.3 % M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}=2.3\% lies approximately 2 dex above the extrapolated local relation between black-hole mass and host stellar mass, suggesting that black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed stellar component. If black-hole growth began only when the first 10% of the observed stellar mass had formed ( t 10 = 92 t_{10}=92 Myr in lookback time) a 10 2 ​ M ⊙ 10^{2}\,M_{\odot} seed would require a lifetime-mean Eddington ratio ⟨ λ ⟩ ≃ 5.7 \langle\lambda\rangle\simeq 5.7 ; earlier growth or a more massive, e.g. direct-collapse black hole, seed would allow more moderate, sub-Eddington mean accretion. In addition, MUSE data reveal extended Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission ( ≃ 6.5 \simeq 6.5 –6.9 proper kpc), offset by + 64 − 8 + 10 +64^{+10}_{-8} km s -1 from systemic, with a provisional escape fraction of ≃ 0.44 \simeq 0.44 . Together with the narrow Mg II doublet ratio close to the optically thin limit and a high [O iii ]/[O ii ] ratio, these properties make MARTA 3887 a system in which black-hole growth, stellar assembly, and ionizing-photon escape can be studied jointly. keywords galaxies: active – galaxies: high-redshift – galaxies: dwarf – galaxies: abundances 1 Introduction The origin of the first massive black holes remains a central problem in galaxy evolution. The existence of ∼ 10 9 ​ M ⊙ {\sim}10^{9}\,M_{\odot} quasars within the first billion years requires massive seeds, sustained near-Eddington accretion, super-Eddington episodes, or a combination of these processes ( Inayoshi et al., 2020 ) . Luminous quasars, however, sample only the high-mass tail of the distribution, while black holes with M BH ∼ 10 5 M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{5} – 10 7 ​ M ⊙ 10^{7}\,M_{\odot} in lower-mass galaxies provide complementary constraints on the early phases of seeding and black-hole-galaxy co-evolution. JWST/NIRSpec has extended the search and characterization of early black holes exactly into this regime. Broad-line AGN with M BH ∼ 10 6 M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{6} – 10 8 ​ M ⊙ 10^{8}\,M_{\odot} are now being routinely identified at high redshift, well below the luminosities accessible to pre-JWST quasar surveys ( Harikane et al., 2023 ; Kocevski et al., 2023 ; Larson et al., 2023 ; Übler et al., 2023 ; Matthee et al., 2024 ; Maiolino et al., 2024a ; Greene et al., 2024 ; Juodžbalis et al., 2026 ; Geris et al., 2026 ) . Many of the newly discovered black holes have large inferred M BH / M ⋆ M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star} ratios relative to local scaling relations ( Reines & Volonteri, 2015 ; Kormendy & Ho, 2013 ; Pacucci et al., 2023 ) , suggesting that black-hole growth might precede the assembly of the dominant stellar component. Strong selection effects related to flux and line-width sensitivity thresholds favour the detection of massive and/or rapidly accreting black holes at fixed host mass, while measurement scatter further enhances the detected upper envelope ( Lauer et al., 2007 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Selection-aware analyses indicate that the intrinsic high-redshift M BH M_{\rm BH} – M ⋆ M_{\star} relation may be consistent with the local relation, but with substantially larger scatter capable of producing the observed high- M BH / M ⋆ M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star} tail ( Ziparo et al., 2026 ) . Even if individual detections preferentially sample this upper envelope, the existence and frequency of such overmassive systems remain informative about black-hole formation and early growth. Models predict different low-mass distributions and scatter depending on their prescriptions for seeding, accretion, and feedback ( Habouzit et al., 2022 ; Volonteri et al., 2023 ; Trinca et al., 2026 ) ; well-characterized systems at the boundaries of the observed parameter space therefore provide complementary constraints on these processes. The identification of the faintest candidates requires particular care. Broad Balmer emission without an associated forbidden-line component of comparable width is a standard signature of a broad-line region (BLR), but at low luminosity it can also arise from interacting supernovae, shocks, outflows, or spatially unresolved galaxy structure ( Maiolino et al., 2025 ; Geris et al., 2026 ) . Classical optical narrow-line diagnostics are also poorly discriminating in the metal-poor, highly ionized ISM regime common at high redshift: metal-poor narrow-line regions overlap with the star-forming sequence, while extreme stellar populations can approach classical AGN-classification boundaries ( Feltre et al., 2016 ; Gutkin et al., 2016 ; Kewley et al., 2013 ; Mazzolari et al., 2024 ) . The combined effect of accretion supplying additional hard ionizing photons and radiative or mechanical AGN feedback lowering the neutral-gas covering fraction could open channels through which both AGN- and stellar-produced Lyman-continuum (LyC) photons can escape. However, this is not an inevitable consequence of hosting an AGN: simulations of high-redshift dwarf galaxies find that supernova feedback can dominate the structure of the ISM and that black-hole activity does not necessarily increase the LyC escape fraction ( Trebitsch et al., 2018 ) . Direct measurements at z ≃ 3 z\simeq 3 –4 span a broad range, from sub-unity average escape fractions in moderate-luminosity AGN to high values in luminous quasars ( Grazian et al., 2018 ; Iwata et al., 2022 ) . Compactness, high [O iii ]/[O ii ], and the presence of strong emission in resonant lines such as Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha and Mg II probing the physical conditions associated with low neutral gas column densities or porous sightlines can therefore test whether active black-hole growth coexists with favourable ionizing radiation escape channels ( Jaskot & Oey, 2013 ; Nakajima & Ouchi, 2014 ; Verhamme et al., 2015 ; Henry et al., 2018 ; Chisholm et al., 2020 ; Izotov et al., 2018 ; Flury et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Naidu et al., 2022 ) . Systems combining these features offer a view of the interplay between black-hole growth, stellar feedback, and ionizing radiation escape. Each proxy remains degenerate with stellar age, dust, gas geometry, and viewing angle, producing substantial scatter with f esc LyC f_{\rm esc}^{\rm LyC} ( Katz et al., 2022 ; Choustikov et al., 2024 ) . In this paper we present a multi-wavelength analysis of MARTA 3887, a compact, clumpy, and metal-poor galaxy at z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 with robust evidence for a low-mass black hole candidate, combining deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy. We investigate the origin of the detected H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha broad component, place the inferred black hole and host properties on scaling relations, and examine the implications for black-hole-galaxy co-evolution and for LyC escape. The paper is organized as follows. Sections 2 – 5 describe the data and measurements, Sect. 6 discusses the AGN interpretation, black-hole growth, and ionizing escape, and the final section summarizes our conclusions. We adopt the Planck 2018 cosmology throughout ( Planck Collaboration et al., 2020 ) . At z = 3.7694 z=3.7694 , 1 ′′ 1^{\prime\prime} corresponds to 7.28 proper kpc. Each scale bar corresponds to 1 proper kpc at the source redshift. 2 Data 2.1 MARTA NIRSpec spectroscopy MARTA (Measuring Abundances at high Redshift with the T e T_{\rm e} Approach) is a JWST Cycle 1 GO programme (PID 1879, PI Curti) designed to obtain high-S/N rest-frame optical spectra of galaxies at cosmic noon and directly constrain their chemical abundances through faint auroral lines ( Cataldi et al., 2025 ) . A single JWST/NIRSpec micro-shutter-array (MSA) pointing in the COSMOS field targeted 127 galaxies ( Gardner et al., 2023 ; Rigby et al., 2023 ; Jakobsen et al., 2022 ; Ferruit et al., 2022 ) . The observing strategy combined a very deep G140M/F100LP exposure (31.6 h), optimized for [O iii ] λ ​ 4363 \lambda 4363 , with G235M/F170LP (7.3 h) coverage of the redder rest-optical spectrum and a shorter G235H/F170LP exposure (2.9 h) for resolved line kinematics. All configurations used three-shutter slitlets and a three-position nod along the slitlet. We reduced the data with the pipeline developed by the NIRSpec Instrument Team, adopted by the JADES collaboration, and described by Scholtz et al. (2026) 1 1 1 Fully reduced data for this programme can be found at https://jades.herts.ac.uk/other_GO/ . . Starting from the calibrated count-rate exposures, the workflow identifies contaminated or non-operational shutters, subtracts the background at pixel level using uncontaminated nod positions, extracts each target trace, applies the wavelength and spectrophotometric calibrations, rectifies and combines the exposures, and produces calibrated two- and one-dimensional spectra. The one-dimensional products use the standard point-source path-loss and slit-loss corrections; we retain the two-dimensional spectra to assess the resolved trace independently in Sect. 3 and Appendix B . A relevant feature of this reduction is the extraction and calibration of spectral traces beyond the nominal wavelength limits of each disperser/filter pair, wherever the detector still records non-negligible throughput. For G235M/F170LP the calibrated range is extended from the nominal red limit near 3.1 ​ μ 3.1\,\mu m to approximately 4.0 ​ μ 4.0\,\mu m ( Scholtz et al., 2026 ) . The final reduced spectra provide therefore usable coverage over 0.97 0.97 – 1.89 ​ μ 1.89\,\mu m, 1.70 1.70 – 4.00 ​ μ 4.00\,\mu m, and 1.66 1.66 – 2.97 ​ μ 2.97\,\mu m, respectively. G140M contains the rest-UV and blue rest-optical lines, G235M includes H ​ β {\rm H}\beta , [O iii ], and recovers the complete H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha +[N ii ] complex, while G235H provides higher-resolution coverage of H ​ β {\rm H}\beta and [O iii ] but does not cover H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha for this target (due to the detector gap). 2.2 HST and JWST imaging The imaging data were retrieved from the version-7 mosaics assembled by the Dawn JWST Archive (DJA; Valentino et al. 2023 ; Brammer et al. 2025 ) . These mosaics combine all publicly available exposures at the target position on a common astrometric grid; the photometry used in this work is measured directly from the science and inverse-variance images. The principal broad-band NIRCam coverage ( Rieke et al., 2023 ) comes from PRIMER (PID 1837; Dunlop et al. 2021 ) and COSMOS-Web (PID 1727; Casey et al. 2023 ), with additional imaging from Blue Jay (PID 1810; Belli et al. 2026 ), COSMOS-3D (PID 5893), and MINERVA (PID 7814; Muzzin et al. 2025 ). Together these data provide NIRCam imaging from F090W to F460M. The DJA products also include archival HST/WFC3 and ACS imaging from F336W to F160W in the COSMOS field ( Scoville et al., 2007 ; Grogin et al., 2011 ; Koekemoer et al., 2011 ) , and MIRI imaging ( Wright et al., 2023 ) in F770W, F1000W, F1280W, F1500W, F1800W, and F2100W. Section 4 describes the image-level quality control, PSF treatment, aperture measurements, and the subset adopted for stellar-population fitting. Figure 1 shows the NIRCam imaging and NIRSpec/MSA footprint for MARTA 3887, with the target located in the central shutter and the three-point nodding pattern sampling five effective shutter positions on the sky. The native RGB image (panel (a)) emphasizes small-scale morphology, while the F444W-PSF-matched rendering (panel (b)) enables a consistent comparison of the light distribution across bands, albeit at reduced angular resolution. NIRCam imaging depicts MARTA 3887 as a multi-component system, with two knots of comparable brightness intercepted by the MSA spectroscopic aperture, and a fainter, southern knot outside of it; such a three-component nature is better seen at the highest resolution of short wavelength filters, as highlighted by the F150W-view of the system shown in panel (c) of Figure 1 (see also Sect. 4.1 and the full list of imaging cutouts in Appendix D.1 ). We note that, at the MSA slit orientation, the bright clumps have overlapping spatial profiles in the extracted NIRSpec spectra, and we therefore treat the one-dimensional spectrum as an integrated measurement of the two. 2.3 Archival VLT/MUSE spectroscopy MARTA 3887 lies within the public MUSE-Wide pointing candels-cosmos-16 ( Bacon et al., 2010 ; Herenz et al., 2017 ; Urrutia et al., 2019 ) . We retrieved the reduced datacube from the ESO Science Archive (programme 097.A-0160(A), dataset ADP.2017-06-19T11:53:53.311). The fiducial full-depth cube combines two independently reduced observing stacks with different seeing. It has an effective on-source exposure time of 3867 s and covers 4749.5 4749.5 – 9349.5 9349.5 Å with a spectral sampling of 1.25 Å pixel -1 and a spatial sampling of 0.2 ′′ 0.2^{\prime\prime} pixel -1 . We use the full-depth cube for all fiducial measurements and the two constituent stacks only for robustness tests described in Appendix E . At the redshift of MARTA 3887 this range contains Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha and the principal rest-UV emission lines (which are, however, undetected, see Appendix E ). The astrometric correction and data processing of the MUSE datacube are outlined in Appendix E , while spectral extraction and spatial analysis of the Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha emission are discussed in Sect. 5 . We note that no other rest-UV line beyond Ly ​ α {\rm Ly}\alpha is robustly detected in the MUSE datacube; the apparent He II λ ​ 1640 \lambda 1640 feature is identified as a sky-subtraction residual through the independent-exposure tests described in Appendix E . 3 NIRSpec emission-line results 3.1 Broad H α \alpha We fit the rest-frame λ ≃ 6450 \lambda\simeq 6450 – 6750 6750 Å region of the G235M spectrum using a local linear continuum and Gaussian emission-line components. Narrow H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha , [N ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 6548 , 6584 \lambda\lambda 6548,6584 , and [S ii ] λ ​ λ ​ 6718 , 6732 \lambda\lambda 6718,6732 share a common velocity and intrinsic dispersion; the [N ii ] doublet ratio is fixed to its atomic value. A second Gaussian is included to model any broad component for the (permitted) H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha emission. All components are convolved with the NIRSpec LSF before comparison with the data. The fit in Fig. 2 detects a broad H ​ α {\rm H}\alpha component with fiducial flux F H ​ α , b = 1.69 × 10 − 18 ​ erg ​ s − 1 ​ cm − 2 F_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1.69\times 10^{-18}\ {\rm erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}} , luminosity L H ​ α , b = 2.35 × 10 41 L_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=2.35\times 10^{41} erg s -1 , and intrinsic FWHM H ​ α , b ≃ 1270 {\rm FWHM}_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}\simeq 1270 km s -1 . Adopting the reference best fit as the fiducial central value, bootstrap refits give F H ​ α , b = 1.69 − 0.19 + 0.26 × 10 − 18 F_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1.69^{+0.26}_{-0.19}\times 10^{-18} erg s -1 cm -2 and FWHM H ​ α , b = 1270 − 250 + 260 {\rm FWHM}_{{\rm H}\alpha,{\rm b}}=1270^{+260}_{-250} km s -1 . The broad model is preferred to a narrow-only model by the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC; lower values are preferred), with Δ ​ BIC = − 46.8 \Delta{\rm BIC}=-46.8 . The two gratings are fitted simultaneously with unite ( Hviding, 2025 ) , a package for the joint forward modeling of spectra from multiple gratings which includes a proper treatment of the LSFs and a relative flux-calibration nuisance parameter; in our model, we specifically assume shared narrow-line kinematics among the lines, while also including an ‘intermediate-width’ [O iii ] component to capture any faint non-core emission. We assume for each grating the LSF for a uniformly illuminated slit ( Jakobsen et al., 2022 ) , and allow a shared multiplicative correction factor to account for any deviation from the nominal resolving power; the fit prefers R scale = 1.086 ± 0.007 R_{\rm scale}=1.086\pm 0.007 for the G235M+G235H fit. We treat it as a phenomenological non-core component: while its modest blueshift is compatible with a low-velocity ionized-gas outflow, we note that unresolved kinematic structure within the clumpy source or residual mismatch between the true LSF and the uniformly illuminated-slit prescription could also contribute to the overall line profile. After marginalizing over the H α \alpha -informed width prior and the uniform − 200 < Δ ​ v < + 200 -200<\Delta v<+200 km s -1 prior adopted above, the broad-H β \beta limit provides no positive lower bound on A V , broad A_{V,{\rm broad}} . We therefore treat the broad H β \beta only as an upper limit and apply no extinction correction to the broad H α \alpha luminosity.
